articles.title: A US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled - Boston Herald
articles.summary: A US-brokered ceasefire was supposed to end the war in Gaza. A year later, progress has stalled  Boston Herald
articles.full_text:
By JOSEPH KRAUSS
It’s been a year since a ceasefire deal brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump and Arab allies promised to end the war in Gaza, and Israel is still launching deadly strikes on the devastated territory.
The agreement halted major military operations, freed all remaining hostages and increased humanitarian access. But it has failed to deliver on promises of a new Palestinian administration aided by international forces, the disarmament of Hamas and an end to Israel’s control over more than half the territory. Almost nothing has been rebuilt.
Israel has tied any progress on the other issues to Hamas’ complete disarmament, while the militant group — and the Trump administration — say they should happen simultaneously. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hardened his stance over the summer, openly defying Trump, his most important ally, ahead of Israeli elections later this month.
The wrangling has left Gaza’s 2 million Palestinians in limbo. Most are sheltering in rodent-infested tent camps, the rubble of their former neighborhoods or war-damaged buildings at risk of collapse.
In the Jabaliya area of the northern Gaza Strip, Abdullah Abu Zubaida’s family lives in a makeshift shelter built from the debris of their house.
“When the ceasefire began last October, we expected the war to halt, assassinations to cease, and aid to flow in,” he said. None of that has happened.
For Ne’man Abu Jarad and his family, displaced from Beit Lahia in northern Gaza to Khan Younis in the south, the truce also has brought no clear path home. The family, including five daughters, continues to live in tents.
“The ceasefire is merely nominal, ink on paper,” Abu Jarad said.
Early success raised hopes of ending the war
The 20-point ceasefire agreement, reached after months of negotiations under the Biden and Trump administrations, ended major military operations and led to the return of all the remaining hostages taken in Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attack that ignited the war.
Hamas fighters killed some 1,200 people that day and abducted 251. Israel responded with massive bombardment and a ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.
After the deal was announced, Trump called for a new era of harmony in the Middle East. “We have a once-in-a-lifetime chance to put the old feuds and bitter hatreds behind us,” he said at a summit marking the deal.
The agreement called for much more
The agreement called for Hamas to hand over power to a committee of Palestinian administrators vetted by the Board of Peace, a new body chaired by Trump and charged with implementing the ceasefire.
Hamas officially dissolved their government in July but left the civil service intact and remain the dominant power in the roughly 40% of Gaza not controlled by the Israeli military. Israel has meanwhile barred the new Palestinian administration from entering Gaza via Egypt.
The formation of an International Stabilization Force was announced in February but has yet to materialize. Indonesia, which pledged the largest troop contingent — 8,000 soldiers — put those plans on hold last spring as the world’s focus shifted to the Iran war.
Israel was supposed to withdraw from Gaza but has instead seized more territory, pushing the so-called yellow Line of Control westward toward the Mediterranean Sea. It has also carried out regular strikes on individuals it accused of violating the ceasefire, approaching the yellow line or having taken part in the Oct. 7 attack — strikes that have often killed civilians.
Israeli strikes have killed over 1,400 Palestinians since the ceasefire took effect, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Sporadic attacks have killed five Israeli soldiers in Gaza in the same period.
More deadlock after Netanyahu defied Trump
In July, Trump announced a deal to disarm Hamas, portraying it as a breakthrough in the long-stalled process.
That deal, an extension of the original ceasefire, called for Hamas to disarm “in a gradual, sequential and time-bound manner” that is “linked to an Israeli withdrawal, in phases.” Hamas confirmed for the first time that it had agreed to disarm, also linking it to Israel halting its strikes and withdrawing from Gaza.
Days later, Netanyahu announced that Israel would not withdraw from any part of Gaza until after Hamas has been completely disarmed, explicitly rejecting the agreement announced by Trump.
The rare instance of friction between the two allies came as Netanyahu seeks to shore up his nationalist base ahead of Oct. 27 elections that could end his nearly unbroken 17-year rule, the longest in Israel’s history.
Netanyahu has come under fire over security and intelligence failures leading up to the Oct. 7 attack, with opponents accusing him of having been soft on Hamas. That gives him little space to make even minor compromises on Gaza, at least until a new government is formed, which could take months.
In the meantime, virtually nothing has been rebuilt in Gaza, Hamas is weakened but still in power, and a return to fighting cannot be ruled out.
Associated Press journalist Wafaa Shurafa in Jabaliya, Gaza Strip, contributed to this report.

articles.summary: On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged  BBCPeace in Yemen runs through the South  GIS ReportsAl-Mahrami calls on Yemeni forces to continue fighting against the Houthis and praises the coalition’s support  Arab NewsCouncil of Ministers Praises Armed Forces Heroic Fighting for Restoring State Institutions  www.sabanew.netYemen is Spiralling into Another Civil War that Could Swiftly Engulf in the Entire Region  ...
articles.full_text:
It was a journey at high speed through the desert - in a pick-up truck with armed fighters in the back. We were travelling with Yemen's pro-government forces, catching glimpses of the Arabian Sea, and forbidding mountain peaks in the distance. Houthi rebels were dislodged from here just days ago, we were told.
When you are battling over expanses of empty desert, progress can be hard to see. But these soldiers, in Shaab-al-Jinn in Lahj governorate, showed us new sandbagged defences - new lines in the sand.
"There was heavy fighting," said Tawfiq Al Haboun, a bearded commander in camouflage uniform.
"They have snipers, artillery and ballistic missile launchers."
Here in the far corners of the Middle East, a war is being waged with global implications.
Yemen's entrenched civil war is now impossible to ignore. It's part of a wider conflict, stretching from Tehran to Riyadh, where missiles slammed into the international airport this weekend. Yemen's Houthi fighters – already a threat to global shipping – are an increasing threat to Saudi Arabia. And they provide leverage for their backers in Iran, Saudi's regional rival.
Tawfiq Al Haboun pointed to shards of fibre glass and bits of metal at his feet – part of a downed Houthi drone that he said was carrying C4 explosives.
Commander Al Haboun is from the Southern Forces, part of the loose – very loose – alliance of groups fighting for Yemen's government, which is internationally recognised, and backed by Saudi Arabia and its air strikes.
The Houthis swept into the capital, Sanaa, in 2014, ousting the government. A year later a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened, trying to dislodge the Houthis. Despite years of devastating air strikes, that hasn't worked.
The commander tells us about 500 Houthi fighters remain on high ground overlooking a strategic maritime corridor – Bab al-Mandab – connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
The narrow waterway, which is crucial for oil exports, was just out of sight on our trip.
The Houthis seized the area after a lightning advance in September. The commander claims pro-government forces have wrested back about 85% (the Houthis have denied losing territory in other areas but not here, as far as our local sources know).
Until they regain complete control, there will be pressure on global oil supplies and on prices.
We heard later that there were heavy clashes the day of our visit. Five military vehicles apparently hit improvised explosive devices planted by the Houthis. It's unclear how many fighters were killed or injured.
As jitters run through international energy markets, hunger menaces weary Yemenis forced to flee this latest spasm of violence.
Around 200,000 have been driven from their homes since the start of this escalation at the beginning of September, according to the International Organization for Migration - all this in the Arab world's poorest country.
As we left the area, we saw a tableau of suffering with families dotted around seeking shelter under scrawny trees. Among one group of women and children we met Aisha, gaunt and elderly and sitting on the ground.
She fled in fear from her home in the Kahboob mountains – an area which has been hit by Houthi drone strikes.
"We have been here for 30 days," she told me.
"I have no animals, no money, no water, no food, not even a blanket... we had to run, with just the clothes on our backs."
At the weekend it was Saudi civilians at the international airport in Riyadh who were doing the running. The Houthi attack - the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade - sent shockwaves around the region and punctured the kingdom's sense of security.
But in operating rooms in Yemen's port city of Aden, geopolitics feels remote. Hospitals are overstretched and doctors are working night and day to treat wounded government fighters coming from the front lines.
We visited one military hospital where 51 casualties arrived in a single day – many with gunshot wounds, and several needing amputations.
In a crowded ward, a Houthi fighter lay alongside fighters from the other side. Doctors tell us they make no distinctions.
"I don't care where he comes from, his background or his religion. He is a human being so I should treat him as a human being, "said Dr Bassam Hazar.
Even if the war ends, some will never leave it behind. One man was sitting silently on his bed, a white bandage wrapped around the stump of his left arm, and staples running along his crown.
Others have not lost their fighting spirit, like Ahmed Ali Mahmoud who is smiling and animated, despite multiple fractures.
"I am not waiting to be fully recovered," he tells us.
"I just want to be able to stand. I think it is a religious duty and a national duty [to go back to fight]. The Houthis have destroyed the country. With victory I won't even feel these fractures."
In the next ward lies 12-year-old Ali, a brown-haired boy, who is just one year older than Yemen's civil war. Ali was injured by a drone as he walked down the street and is facing a complicated surgery.
"There is shrapnel near his spine," says Dr Amr Reyadh Assaqaf, standing by his bedside.
"The operation won't be easy, but God willing our staff will be able to handle it."
He tells me Ali is quiet and gentle.
"At first he was depressed," he says, "but we gave him toys to play with and his mood is gradually lifting."
But will war follow him into adulthood?
A truce in 2022 brought a few years of relative calm. But now the Houthis are a stronger enemy, as they have proven at the weekend. They already control most of Yemen's population. If there is a new attempt at mediation – and there is some speculation about this - they may drive a hard bargain.
Back at the hospital, as he prepares for the next wave of casualties, Dr Bassam Hazar hopes for change but doesn't expect it soon.
"Maybe war is good for news," he says, "but it's horrible [for people].
"Sons are losing their fathers, and mothers losing their sons. We need peace."
Additional reporting by Wietske Burema, Rawa Gorgorh, Lee Durant and Suaad Al Salahi
All pictures by Lee Durant.
Correction 12 October: We initially reported that Aisha had said she was scared of Saudi air strikes. This was down to a translation error. In fact it was Houthi drone strikes that had been hitting her area.

articles.title: Singapore refreshes cyber strategy with new national tool to block malware and phishing sites - British Chamber Of Commerce Singapore
articles.summary: Singapore refreshes cyber strategy with new national tool to block malware and phishing sites  British Chamber Of Commerce Singapore
articles.full_text:
Senior Minister K Shanmugam, who is also Coordinating Minister for National Security and Home Affairs Minister, delivering the opening address at the Singapore International Cyber Week 2026 on Oct 13. (ST PHOTO: KEVIN LIM)
Source: The Straits Times
A new national service will soon block Singapore users from accessing known phishing and malware sites amid a sharp rise in the number of infected computer systems here.
Called a protective domain name service (PDNS), it was announced on Oct 13 by Senior Minister K. Shanmugam as part of Singapore’s refreshed cybersecurity strategy to counter heightened cyber threats.
The shift is toward a proactive, AI-driven national defence model as threat actors have become faster and more sophisticated thanks to artificial intelligence.
“Singapore will seek to act earlier, act at national scale and act at the speed of the threat. This shift is an important part of Singapore’s cybersecurity strategy 2026 which we are launching today,” said Shanmugam, Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs.
He was speaking at the opening of the 11th Singapore International Cyber Week at the Marina Bay Sands Expo and Convention Centre.
Shanmugam said Singapore’s updated cybersecurity strategy is broader than how national cyberdefence has been viewed so far.
“It will cover how we will strengthen our critical infrastructure in the wider cyberspace, build capabilities for AI and quantum, deepen our global partnerships, and invest in our cybersecurity ecosystem and workforce,” he said.
Expected to be rolled out in 2027, the new PDNS will be operated by the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore’s (CSA) National Cybersecurity Command Centre, under the Online Criminal Harms Act.
The Act, which came into force in 2024, allows the authorities to ask individuals, companies and internet service providers to remove or block access to content that they suspect is being used to commit crimes, such as illegal gambling and money lending, drug-related offences, scams, and malicious cyber activities.
CSA said that the new service will have safeguards to “ensure the responsible exercise” of powers under the Online Criminal Harms Act.
The agency said that a “robust assessment and validation process” will be carried out before malicious websites are blocked, to reduce the risk of false positives and to ensure site blocking decisions can be accounted for.
Individuals or organisations affected by the service’s website blocking can seek recourse through the Act’s existing reconsideration and appeal processes.
Similar malicious-website blocking services have been implemented in Australia, Canada, the European Union, the United Kingdom and the United States.
In 2022, an inter-agency Counter Ransomware Task Force in Singapore recommended the use of PDNS as a form of “upstream defence” to prevent known malicious attackers from reaching internet users here.
This is because such attackers can trick users into downloading malware from malicious sites that can steal users’ company data or lock it up until a ransom is paid.
Navigating cyberspace safely is becoming more difficult. According to CSA’s latest Singapore Cyber Landscape report published in June, the number of malware-infected computer systems detected in Singapore more than doubled to 284,300 in 2025, from 117,300 infected systems detected in 2024.
“Singapore must raise the level of cybersecurity across our entire ecosystem,” said CSA on Oct 13, adding that such upstream protection is one of the key thrusts of the country’s refreshed cybersecurity strategy to counter more frequent and advanced threats.
The other pillars of the national strategy are: defending critical infrastructure; strengthening capabilities for AI and quantum technologies; and improving resilience through global partnerships.
Computer systems of critical infrastructure, or critical information infrastructure like those for power plants and telecommunications, are being increasingly targeted by hackers behind advanced cyberattacks that can stay undetected for long periods of time. These attackers are also called advanced persistent threat actors.
An attack in Singapore by one such group of hackers was revealed in July 2025. The country’s four major telcos were attacked by state-sponsored cyberespionage group UNC3886. The attack could have disrupted telecommunications and internet services had the attackers infiltrated further.
Other new safety measures include exploring cyber insurance pilots, as well as the police setting up a new Cyber Command unit in July to target scammers and cybercriminals before they reach Singaporeans.
“The intensified threat landscape underpins the need for a command centre with enhanced national capabilities to detect cyber risks earlier and accelerate operational responses,” CSA said, referring to its National Cybersecurity Command Centre.
Announced in 2024, the centre detects and neutralises cyber threats before they reach Singapore’s shores.
Besides operating the PDNS, the centre will also allow cyber defenders of critical information infrastructure to combine threat intelligence from various sources to facilitate the coordination of cyber operations at a national level.
The cyber defenders will also be able to detect malicious activities, especially those of advanced persistent threat actors, with a new proprietary threat detection system developed by the Ministry of Defence’s Centre for Strategic Infocomm Technologies. The centre is working with CSA to equip selected infrastructure owners with the systems.
Separate systems will also be deployed that use AI to track ongoing incidents and help cyberdefenders to develop operational assessments and plan their next actions. These will allow the National Cybersecurity Command Centre to coordinate faster responses to cyberincidents.
Wider adoption of AI and migration to quantum-safe systems are also part of Singapore’s refreshed strategy to strengthen protection.
Attackers are using AI tools to strike faster and at greater scale, while advancements in quantum computing threaten to undermine methods used today to encrypt data.

Yet, these nations don’t have the combined economic and military strength needed to resist a coordinated blockade by the world’s biggest economy and its intelligence apparatus.

With the UN and its legal bodies splintering, major powers like China and Russia are seizing the opportunity to shape the situation to their advantage. Instead of upholding the current UN system, they’re pushing global structures toward alternative blocs, such as expanded BRICS, speeding up the shift to a multipolar world driven by transactional partnerships rather than shared legal norms.

Saturday's attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh backs the internationally-recognized government against the Houthis, who captured swaths of Red Sea coastline in a lightning offensive last month.
The strike came in a week when the group intensified its attacks on the Saudi capital's King Khalid International Airport, where three people were also killed on Thursday, as well as other key targets in the world's top crude oil exporter.

Five Ukrainian minehunters have completed seven days of intensive training off the south coast of England, closing with a run in close formation around the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless in the eastern Solent, according to the Royal Navy.
The ships are based in Portsmouth as part of British support to Ukraine, and the training ranged across the Dorset, Hampshire and Isle of Wight coastlines, taking in gunnery, the destruction of dummy mines and formation sailing with a major warship.
UNS Henichesk, Mariupol, Melitopol, Chernihiv and Cherkasy made up the quintet. Under the supervision of British military personnel they first demonstrated their ability to defend themselves with gunnery shoots off Portland, then moved on to locating, identifying and where necessary destroying underwater explosive devices.
That work used Seafox, the remotely operated submersible that has been a mainstay of Royal Navy mine countermeasures for a couple of decades. Chernihiv and Cherkasy both carried out live firings of the system, which ended in controlled explosions neutralising the mine threats they had been set.
The seven days formed the final chapter of Exercise Lion Protector, a Joint Expeditionary Force exercise running from August until the weekend and intended to refine how member nations respond militarily to protect Europe’s northern flank. Its fifth and last phase shifted the emphasis onto the ability of JEF navies to protect maritime infrastructure and guarantee the security of sea lanes.
Earlier phases took the UK Commando Force to the Faroe Islands to work on safeguarding the Greenland, Iceland and United Kingdom gap, the first time Royal Marines have operated in the Atlantic chain since the Second World War. The Royal Navy rates Lion Protector second only to Sea Breeze, the Ukrainian Navy’s premier annual exercise, in scope and complexity. Sea Breeze itself was held off the south coast of England over the summer.
Dauntless played the part of the major warship in the closing serial, with the Ukrainian ships manoeuvring around her as a small task group. The destroyer is preparing to escort the fleet flagship HMS Prince of Wales when she resumes her Firecrest 2026 deployment to the High North. Mine countermeasures have become one of the more practical forms of British help to Ukraine, since the Black Sea remains heavily mined and the Ukrainian Navy has had to rebuild capability.
I wonder what would happen if the Russian frigate that seems to be permanently based in the North sea/channel area attacked these Ukrainian mine hunters, would the RN come to their aid ?
Only if it took place in uk territorial waters. However the Ukrainians are not daft, if they were anywhere near a Russian warship it would be to sink it.
I was just wondering what (if anything) the UK government would do if it kicked off between the Ukrainian naval vessels and the Russian Frigate. The ex RN mine hunters would be no good in a fight against a Frigate (even one as old as the one currently in the Channel) but would make excellent launch platforms for drone’s.
Perhaps we will find out … but I doubt it. Russia will I suspect want to avoid any contact.
Let us hope so.

Across the West there were scores of anti-Israel gatherings on the day Israelis mourned the rape and destruction of more than a thousand of their citizens. There’s an all-out effort to redefine the day that Hamas unleashed genocidal violence on the Jews of the Holy Land as the day ‘Israel’s genocide’ started. The old Nazis stole Jews’ property – the new ones steal their days of commemoration.
Meanwhile, the Green Party of England and Wales voted in favour of the annihilation of the Jewish homeland. They are morally as one with Hamas, which is likewise fuelled by a genocidal urge to scrub Israel from the face of the Earth. The Green Party member who put forward this racist proposal to erase the Jews’ homeland has been exposed as a one-time ‘good friend’ of the al-Qaeda freak who plotted to make a rucksack bomb full of shrapnel dipped in rat poison and then blow himself up at Heathrow Airport with the aim of massacring passengers from Israel. Can we talk about this? The fact that a mainstream party in the UK is taking its moral cues from a member who was mates with an Islamist terrorist who dreamt of murdering Jews? The fact that the ‘anti-fascist’ left is lining up with a party that wants to destroy Israel, and which has members who called Jews cockroaches, and whose deputy leader celebrated the Jew-murder of 7 October with cackles of ‘Allahu Akbar’?
At least they can deny it no longer – their aim is not to end the war in Gaza but to end Israel. Their dream is not peace but annihilation. If the keffiyeh classes got their way, and Israel was dismantled, the consequence would be an extermination of Jews that would make 7 October look like a tea party. To Israel’s south is an army of anti-Semites (Hamas) that openly says it wants to cut off the heads of Jews. To its north is an Islamofascist outfit (Hezbollah) that calls Jews ‘apes and pigs’ and says they should fuck off ‘back to Germany, or wherever they came from’. And to its east is the Islamic Republic, a nation that entirely defines itself by its cosmic hostility to Jewish nationhood. To agitate for the dismantling of Israel in such circumstances is to agitate for the mass expulsion and the mass murder of Jews. Own it.
The longed-for erasure of Israel is justified through the erasure of Jewish history. Owen Jones spent last week arguing that Israel was ‘carved out of a land that was 90 per cent Arab Muslim and Christian’. He’s referring to 1917, the year of the Balfour Declaration. To single out that year without mentioning what preceded it or what followed it is one of the most sinister acts of Orwellian obfuscation I have ever seen from a mainstream journalist.
The reason Jews made up just 10 per cent of the Holy Land in the 1910s is because for centuries they had been violently expelled and violently converted by everyone from the Romans to the Arabs to the Ottomans. And to fail to mention the Fifth Aliyah of 1929 to 1939, when hundreds of thousands of Jews returned to Israel, is criminal. These were not ‘invading Zionists’ but Jews fleeing their ghettoisation, enslavement and burning to death by Nazis. Does Jones think they should have stayed in Europe? The depiction of Israel as a product of ‘Zionist invasion’ is the great lie of our times. In truth, Israel is a wholly anti-colonial enterprise born from the stirring refusal of Jews to be world-scattered targets for Nazi scum and peasant pogromists.
Last week, the mask – or the keffiyeh – truly slipped. Some of us have known since 8 October 2023, and earlier, that the ‘pro-Palestine’ movement is a regressive, bigoted crusade devoted less to the liberation of Palestinians than to the annihilation of Israel. That this is less about making a homeland for the Palestinians and more about dancing on the ashes of the homeland of the Jews. Surely now others can see it too? Anti-Semitism is always a catalyst for civilisational collapse, said Hannah Arendt, as it opens the doors to totalitarian movements. So it is today. Everyone who values reason, truth, liberty and basic human decency should stand with their every fibre against the bourgeois war of annihilation against the Jewish State.

articles.title: UK PM Burnham Says Russia Interfered In Brexit Vote, Warns France And Germany - Arise News
articles.summary: UK PM Burnham Says Russia Interfered In Brexit Vote, Warns France And Germany  Arise News
articles.full_text:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russia interfered in the UK’s 2016 Brexit referendum, revealing that he received confirmation after requesting information about Moscow’s activities when he entered Downing Street.
Burnham said the government had not done enough to inform the public about foreign attempts to influence democratic processes, warning that similar Russian activities were taking place in Germany and France.
Speaking on a podcast, in an interview scheduled for release on Monday, the prime minister said he had specifically asked about possible Russian interference in the Brexit vote after taking office. “I’ve had the clear answer that, yes, there was. I think we’ve been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven’t informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas.”
Burnham did not disclose the nature or scale of Russia’s involvement in the referendum or provide evidence that it affected the final result.
His remarks mark the first time a serving British prime minister has publicly stated that Russia sought to influence the 2016 Brexit vote.
Britain Unbound, a pro-Brexit campaign organisation, criticised the prime minister’s comments, describing them as another crude attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the decision that the British people made in 2016.
The group acknowledged that foreign interference in British elections was unacceptable but disputed suggestions that Russian activities had influenced the referendum’s outcome. “There is no good reason to believe that Russian intervention influenced the outcome of the referendum in 2016. It is also insulting to suggest that voters were so easily duped.”
The prime minister said he had discussed Russian interference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz during a visit to Germany earlier in the week.
He warned that misinformation and disinformation originating from Russia were already affecting German political debate. “There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics.”
He argued that governments needed to be more open about foreign attempts to influence voters, particularly in Germany and France. “These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.”
Burnham’s remarks follow years of warnings about Russian attempts to influence British politics.
In 2020, Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee published a report examining Russian interference in UK elections and referendums.
The committee did not reach a definitive conclusion on whether Russia had attempted to influence the outcome of the Brexit referendum. It criticised successive British governments for failing to adequately investigate or respond to the threat.
Russia rejected the findings, with its foreign minister dismissing the report as an example of “Russophobia.” A Kremlin spokesperson also denied that Moscow interfered in elections held by other countries.
The Conservative government at the time separately concluded that it was almost certain Russian actors had attempted to interfere in the UK’s 2019 general election.
More recently, BBC Verify has tracked Russian-linked disinformation operations involving artificial intelligence-generated videos impersonating journalists and established news organisations.
One campaign used a fake news website to circulate a false claim that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had purchased a mansion belonging to King Charles at a discounted price.
Earlier this year, UK Electoral Commission chief Vijay Rangarajan warned MPs that Russian deepfake videos had been widely used to influence elections internationally.
“There is no reason to assume Britain would be an exception.”
During his address to the United Nations last month, Burnham accused Russian agencies of using disinformation to exploit public fears and undermine democratic institutions.
He announced plans to establish a new UK centre to counter foreign disinformation campaigns.
A Downing Street spokesperson said the government was working to protect British citizens and institutions against foreign powers and their proxies.
“We are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values,” the spokesperson said.
The government said its response included strengthening powers under the National Security Act, improving the security of critical national infrastructure and reinforcing border protection, policing and intelligence capabilities.

articles.title: In Israel’s election, Netanyahu faces a reckoning over Oct. 7 failure - The Forward
articles.summary: In Israel’s election, Netanyahu faces a reckoning over Oct. 7 failure  The ForwardAn Israeli Election Like No Other  The New York TimesBenjamin Netanyahu's legacy and political future on the line in Israel's Oct 27 election  Fox News‘Peace is not in people’s minds’: October 7 scars take center stage for first-time voters  The Times of IsraelIsrael election: Could Naftali Bennett rescue Benjamin Netanyahu from an election deadlock?  The Jerusalem ...
articles.full_text:
Two weeks before Israelis vote, Netanyahu’s former aides deliver explosive testimony, allegations of falsified records and demands for an independent inquiry.
With barely two weeks remaining before Israel’s Oct. 27 election, the country has been consumed by an extraordinary confrontation between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and senior former aides over what he knew before the Hamas massacre of Oct. 7, 2023, what he did with that knowledge and whether his office subsequently sought to rewrite the historical record.
The immediate catalyst was a bombshell television interview in recent days with Maj. Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, Netanyahu’s former military secretary, who served alongside him before and during the attack that killed approximately 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. Gil had remained largely silent for three years, expecting to present his evidence to a state commission of inquiry. But with Netanyahu blocking such an inquiry, amid transparent scheming to deflect blame, Gil decided to speak publicly.
What he described went considerably beyond the failures of intelligence and military preparedness that have already been extensively documented. Gil accused Netanyahu’s office of attempting to falsify an official record from the morning of the attack. He challenged the prime minister’s account of early warnings he received. He confirmed that Netanyahu rejected recommendations for preventive military operations against Hamas. And he described how political considerations influenced decisions over hostage negotiations, potentially prolonging the captivity of people who could have been brought home earlier – and alive.
His testimony is particularly consequential because it directly challenges a 55-page document Netanyahu released in February, presenting his version of the events preceding Oct. 7. Submitted to Israel’s state comptroller, the document portrayed Netanyahu as having repeatedly advocated tougher action against Hamas while security officials underestimated the threat. It has become central to his defense against accusations that his longstanding policy of containing Hamas helped create the conditions for the catastrophe.
Gil, who attended the relevant meetings and recorded his experiences in 16 notebooks, described the published document as a profoundly incomplete and misleading account, containing lies and half-truths. It failed to reflect even half of what he witnessed.
A separate investigation published Friday by Yedioth Ahronoth, comparing Netanyahu’s account with original records of security deliberations, reported significant omissions and distortions, including instances in which Netanyahu allegedly rejected proposals to target Hamas leaders that his February document presented as initiatives of his own.
Most explosive was Gil’s account of an alleged attempt by Netanyahu’s then-chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman, to change the official time of a telephone conversation on Oct. 7 from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m. Moving the time backward could create the impression that Netanyahu had been issuing instructions from the first moments of the assault. Gil said a stenographer told him she had been instructed to alter the record, prompting him to notify the attorney general.
Nitzan Alon, another retired general who headed the government’s hostage release operation, and took part in negotiations throughout much of the war, also told reporters that “it was possible to end the war a year earlier” and save the lives of numerous hostages who eventually died in captivity.
Another remarkable confrontation involves Ronen Bar, the former head of the Shin Bet domestic security agency, whom Netanyahu has repeatedly blamed for the failures of Oct. 7. In late September, Bar announced plans to sue Netanyahu for defamation, accusing him of conducting a campaign of false allegations about his conduct before the massacre. Bar said he had warned Netanyahu about a looming security disaster and demanded disclosure of the original records of security meetings, communications and warnings, including the prime minister’s contacts with foreign officials.
Those demands have acquired additional significance amid reports that senior officials from Egypt and the United Arab Emirates warned Netanyahu about Hamas preparations shortly before the attack. Netanyahu categorically denies receiving such warnings and has threatened legal action over the reporting.
Gil’s revelations arrived alongside another striking intervention from a former Netanyahu confidant. Yoav Horowitz, , once Netanyahu’s chief of staff and director-general of the Prime Minister’s Office, told Kan’s Reshet Bet radio last week that he had gradually come to understand that Netanyahu’s decisions were driven primarily by considerations of personal political survival rather than the national interest.
Now a senior aide to leading opposition figure Gadi Eisenkot, Horowitz attributed that transformation to the corrosive effects of prolonged power, observing that “too much time in power corrupts,” and framed the approaching election as being about saving the country.
Horowitz now heads the team preparing its first 100 days in government. His criticism therefore comes from a former trusted aide who has become an active political opponent, adding another dimension to the dispute over Netanyahu’s leadership.
The question of political survival also figured prominently in Gil’s account of the hostage negotiations. Asked whether coalition pressures had influenced decisions that delayed agreements to free hostages, Gil said some hostages could have returned earlier and that political calculations had played a role in the decisions that kept them in captivity.
Netanyahu has rejected Gil’s allegations, and his Likud party has characterized the latest revelations as politically motivated propaganda. Netanyahu and his supporters maintain that senior security officials failed to recognize the imminent danger.
The country is still struggling to establish a common factual account of its most traumatic day in decades, while the officials who participated in the crucial decisions offer sharply conflicting versions of what happened. Meanwhile, the families of those killed on Oct. 7, survivors of the massacre and former hostages continue demanding answers about the decisions that shaped their lives.
The public appetite for an inquiry into the disaster is overwhelming. A September 2025 survey by the Israel Democracy Institute found that 74 percent of Israelis supported establishing a state commission of inquiry, including 68 percent of Jewish respondents identifying with the political right. A subsequent survey conducted in February 2026 found that 92 percent of Israelis considered it important to investigate the events.
The absence of such an inquiry has left journalists, former officials, politicians and bereaved families conducting an increasingly contentious public investigation of their own. Documents appear selectively, witnesses offer competing recollections, and allegations that might otherwise be tested through sworn testimony and access to classified evidence become weapons in an election campaign. With spiraling suspicions being leveled at Netanyahu, the election will take place amid unresolved questions – and a rage that grows more toxic by the day.

The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences has been awarded to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for developing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”
Nobel Prize for Economics awarded to Hall and Woodford
Newsflash: The Nobel Prize for economicshas been awarded to Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford, for their work on the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”.
[Reminder: As we flagged earlier, Woodford was among the predicted winners – he’s one of the architects of modern forward guidance, the idea that central banks can control the economy through influencing public expectations about inflation, rather than just through interest rates.]
The Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel is worth 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000), plus the glory of course, and the knowledge that every pronouncement you make now comes with the authority of a Nobel Prize winner.
Two US economists have won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work developing models that help central bankers and finance ministers to stabilise their countries, avoiding long recessions and runaway inflation.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said it was recognising the pair for generating “a paradigm shift in stabilisation policy”, awarding them the prize worth a combined $1.2m (£900,000).
“New Keynesian models, a result of their research, allow us to explain and quantify how stabilisation policy affects business cycles and are now used by central banks and finance ministries around the world,” the academy said.
Here’s the full story:
In other news….
The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year.
Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said, as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI.
Millions of British van drivers face a combined £2.5bn cost to cover the rising price of diesel this year, according to figures, fuelling calls for the government to scrap its planned fuel duty rise.
John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures.
The euro is having a bad day, dropping to a 16-month low against the pound.
Expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates next month appear to have lifted the pound to €1.1836, the highest since June 2025.
Enrique Díaz-Alvarez, chief economist at global financial services firm Ebury, says:
“The sterling rally against the common currency continues to hit fresh 16-month highs, with the pound also stabilising against the US dollar.
“As in the previous week, this was more about the euro’s troubles than about any good news in Britain. Markets increasingly expect the Bank of England to raise rates at its 5th November meeting and we concur, though we still see this as no more than a one off insurance hike. We will this week hear from MPC members Mann, Greene and Pill - the three members who voted for a hike in September.
HMV to quit historic Oxford Street store, again....
Sarah Butler
Away from the Nobel economics prize announcement….HMV is preparing to exit its London flagship on Oxford Street in March - just over three years after reopening there with great fanfair – as the landlord proposed doubling the rent.
The entertainment retailer said it was now seeking alternative sites on the capital’s main high street, or another central location, as it had been trading strongly, my colleague Sarah Butler reports.
The latest closure comes after HMVreturned to the site in November 2023 after closing in 2019 leaving the store empty for an extended period before a brief stint housing one of many American candy stores that popped up on Oxford Street during the pandemic.
HMV, which currently has 114 stores under its own brand across the UK and a further six Fopp sites, said a proposed increase in rent which is already understood to be well over £1m a year – coupled with a requirement to fund substantial renovation works on the Oxford Street building – would make the store “commercially unsustainable”, leaving it with no choice but to seek an alternative site.
The store was HMV’s very first, and was opened in 1921 by Sir Edward Elgar, the British composer. Since then it has played host to a number of British bands, including a rooftop gig by Blur in 1995 and the Spice Girls’ Christmas lights switch-on the following year.
It is understood the Hong Kong-based landlord has signed a lease with an alternative tenant.
PhilHalliday, managing director of HMV, said:
“This is a special store, it’s where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history. It’s frustrating that it has been made commercially unviable. However, we are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for hmv in 2027.”
He said sales were up by a quarter year-on-year at the Oxford Street store and 15% at established UK stores in the first nine months of 2026 as sales of both vinyl records and CDs continued to sell well and more shoppers came into stores.
“We have put together an offer that works across a number of generations,” Halliday added.
The retailer is expecting UK revenues to exceed £240m this year across the stores estate and website, up from £212m in 2025. The business now generates £50m of sales online and is upgrading its website backed by a new warehouse set to open next year.
“We’ve worked hard to make 363 Oxford Street a destination for pop-culture fans, bringing live performances, artist signings and a huge range of music and entertainment back to the heart of London. However, regardless of how much a location means to us, it has to make commercial sense.” Halliday said.
He said HMV intended to redeploy affected staff through other London stores and Head Office roles.
After learning of his success, Michael Woodford was asked during today’s press conference if any economic event or shock had ensured that his new framework had really stood up to the test.
Bloomberg has the details:
He cited how central banks adapted their toolkit to the global financial crisis of 2008 as they confronted a slump in demand that reductions in borrowing costs on their own couldn’t solve.
“Forward guidance about policy, so making more explicit statements about the likely future path of interest rate policy as opposed to relying on simply being able to cut interest rates further immediately — that was an important part of the policy response,” he said.
“It did contribute to better stabilization. It didn’t magically solve the problem, but I think it was an important contribution.”
Here’s how John Hassler, chair of the prize committee, announced Hall and Woodford’s success this morning:
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,”
“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.”
Over at FT Alphaville, Toby Nangle has described Michael Woodford is “probably the most famous New Keynesian economist”.
Nangle (formally a senior asset manager at ColumbiaThreadneedle) writes:
If you’re friends with at least one econ nerd, you’ve probably heard either love or hate for Woodford’s Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy dropped into dinner-party conversations. This is his reputation-defining tome, named cheekily to echo Knut Wicksell’s Interest and Prices, written more than a century previously.
Woodford basically rebuilt Wicksell’s insights around the relationship between interest rates and the economy’s natural interest rate using modern general equilibrium economics.
And today, almost all central banks run dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models incorporating Woodfordian insights, including the Fed, the ECB, the Bank of England, and the mother of them all: Sveriges Riksbank.
Following today’s announcement, the Nobel prize for economics has now been awarded on 58 occasions.
That dates back to 1969, when RagnarFrisch and JanTinbergen won it “for having developed and applied dynamic models for the analysis of economic processes”.
The oldest winner was LeonidHurwicz, who was 90 in 2007 when he won alongside EricMaskin and RogerMyerson “for having laid the foundations of mechanism design theory”.
The youngest remains EstherDuflo, who was just 46 in 2019 when she shared the prize with AbhijitBanerjee and MichaelKremer. “for their experimental approach to alleviating global poverty” (as we blogged here).
Praise for Woodford and Hall is starting to pour in
Analytics company Clarivate, which had awarded both RobertHall and MichaelWoodford one of its Citations Laureate – given to those who are considered likely to win the Nobel Prize due to their research expertise – says today’s award is certainly merited.
DavidPendlebury, head of research analysis, institute for scientific information at Clarivate, explains:
“We are delighted to see both Robert Hall and Michael Woodford recognized with this year’s Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences. Hall was named a Citation Laureate in 2017 and Woodford earlier this year in 2026, reflecting the exceptional influence of their research. Their work has fundamentally shaped modern thinking about economic stabilization, productivity, economic fluctuations and the role of monetary policy in supporting economic growth and stability.
Looking at the publication record in the Web of Science, we see the enduring impact of their contributions. Their research has influenced generations of economists and helped inform economic policymaking around the world, demonstrating how foundational ideas can shape both academic understanding and real-world decision-making for decades.”

articles.title: Chinese Robots Could Decide the AI Race
articles.summary: Scott Singer and Pavlo Zvenyhorodsky, researchers at Carnegie’s China AI Initiative, argue that China is betting that AI dominance will come from combining hardware and software, or AI-powered robots. By focusing only on software such as AI models, they argue, Washington and Silicon Valley risk falling behind.
articles.full_text:
The fastest track and field athlete is no longer the Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt. In fact, it is not a person at all: it is the Chinese humanoid robot Tiangong Ultra, which in August ran 100 meters in 9.39 seconds, nearly two-tenths of a second faster than Bolt’s world-record time and more than twice as fast as its own time a year ago. The race made global headlines and spread on social media in large part because of what it revealed robots still can’t do—in this case, slow down, as Tiangong Ultra ran right through the finish line and slammed into a safety wall. But it also showcased the incredible progress China’s robotics industry has made and the narrowing gap between human capabilities and new technology.
China’s robotics achievements have become central to its evolving national AI strategy. Whereas Washington and Silicon Valley focus primarily on scaling large language models and digital AI applications, Beijing is concentrating on combining its strengths in software and hardware to develop robots that incorporate the advanced cognition of AI with autonomous physical movement. These robots, often described in China as “embodied AI,” could eventually operate factories, perform manual labor, and even replace human soldiers on the battlefield. If AI-powered robots develop enough autonomy to carry out sophisticated tasks in the real world, they could become a general-purpose technology, like electricity or the Internet, that is able to transform physical work across broad swaths of the economy.
For Beijing, a powerful AI-driven robotics industry could serve several of its economic and strategic goals. It could ease demographic pressures from an aging population by reducing the need for workers and providing eldercare. It could also supercharge Beijing’s military capabilities by automating its reconnaissance, logistics, and combat operations. Most notably, some leading Chinese thinkers believe robotics could be the key to unlocking artificial general intelligence—systems capable of performing as well as or better than humans across most tasks. China’s investments in AI-powered robotics could be especially consequential if today’s leading AI companies in Silicon Valley, which are focused on scaling the data and computing power used to train large models, struggle to translate their digital gains into advancements in the physical world.
Skeptics might think that AI-powered robots are the stuff of science fiction. But as robotics technology rapidly develops, China is betting that some of the most consequential advances in AI will hinge on mastery of the physical world. If that bet is right, even only partially, the United States’ lead in frontier models would matter far less than many in Washington assume. What would matter instead is the capacity to build robots, deploy them in sectors such as manufacturing and logistics, and generate enough data to continuously train them—all areas in which the United States currently underinvests. To compete, Washington needs to expand its own manufacturing sector and work with partners around the world that have developed advantages in key parts of the robotics supply chain. As China sprints ahead, the United States needs to get serious about AI-powered robots or it risks getting left behind.
EMBODIED POSITIVITY
The Chinese government is determined to lead the transformation toward a world of AI-powered robots. Beijing has placed embodied AI among what it calls the “industries of the future,” alongside 6G and quantum technology, and named it a priority in the 15th Five-Year Plan—the country’s socioeconomic blueprint through 2030. Facing high youth unemployment, a property market still in crisis, sluggish domestic consumption, and an aging and shrinking population, Beijing sees embodied AI as a new growth engine that could offset these headwinds while also pushing technological frontiers.
Innovations aimed at addressing domestic challenges could quickly create a geoeconomic advantage. China already controls key chokepoints in the emerging supply chain for embodied AI. Chinese companies, for example, produce about 80 percent of the world’s LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) sensors—the technology that underpins three-dimensional mapping and autonomous navigation in self-driving vehicles, warehouse robots, and precision agricultural tools. If AI-powered robots become as foundational to the global economy as Beijing hopes, countries would be as dependent on Chinese robotics supply chains as they are today for critical minerals, which has given Beijing enormous leverage over the global economy.
The strategic benefits of AI-powered robots extend to the military. In February, the Chinese Institute of Command and Control, a state-connected national scientific society, assessed that embodied AI could enable networks of unmanned systems operating across air, land, sea, and space to share information, anticipate battlefield developments, and carry out precision strikes in real time. This could significantly enhance the ability of the People’s Liberation Army to coordinate joint operations across varied terrain, such as around the disputed islands and outcroppings in the South China Sea.
 Beijing is combining its strengths in software and hardware.
Most important, a growing number of prominent scientists in China have argued that embodied AI could offer a potentially neglected pathway to building artificial general intelligence. Zhang Bo, the founding dean of Tsinghua University’s Institute for Artificial Intelligence and a pioneering AI researcher, has written that intelligence relies not only on cognition but also on the ability to learn from and make decisions in the physical world. Embodied AI, he argues, can overcome the shortcomings of traditional AI and accelerate progress toward AGI. Zhou Bowen, the director and chief scientist at Shanghai AI Lab, one of the country’s leading AI research institutes, has similarly argued that AI models need robotics to understand the physical world. China’s unmatched manufacturing base can become a training ground for artificial intelligence as real-world data feed back into AI systems. The more data these systems acquire on how to navigate complex real-world settings, the better they will perform in new environments and the quicker they can develop.
Beijing’s bet on embodied AI is not a turn away from software or a concession in the software race with Washington. China’s leading labs such as DeepSeek and Z.ai are scaling large language models as aggressively as their American counterparts. Many have begun using AI to automate AI research in the same way U.S. companies have, bringing them closer to what technology experts call “recursive self-improvement”—when highly capable AI is able to continuously build ever more capable AI, which could create a potential intelligence explosion. What sets Beijing apart from Washington is the simultaneous efforts it is making in developing AI in the physical world, where it is far outpacing everyone else.
FROM THE BOT UP
To accelerate the development of AI-powered robots, Beijing has directed local officials to experiment with ways to boost innovation and expand production. Provincial governments, adept at interpreting and carrying out the central leadership’s priorities, have responded rapidly. Wealthy provinces and cities with established high-tech ecosystems, including Beijing, Guangdong, Shanghai, and Zhejiang, have jockeyed aggressively to position themselves as national front-runners. They have established dedicated venture capital funds, introduced subsidy schemes, and set up specialized training facilities to support local AI-powered robotics companies.
This approach mirrors the strategy Beijing successfully used to develop technologies such as electric vehicles and solar energy. Acting on broad policy direction from Beijing, provincial and city officials offered companies generous subsidies, tax breaks, and preferential leases on land. These local governments’ efforts to outdo one another in carrying out Beijing’s strategy yielded widespread overcapacity and huge amounts of waste. Yet it also helped cultivate globally competitive firms, including BYD, which has emerged as the world’s leading electric carmaker.
Financing a boom for AI-powered robots, however, will be more difficult than it was to finance a boom for electric vehicles and solar panels. The property market downturn, which has now lasted five years, has strained local budgets. Governments can no longer rely on selling land-use rights to developers to fill their coffers, taking away one of their main sources of revenue and limiting the funds available to encourage the growth of new industries. Aside from the wealthiest areas, there is not much money available for robotics.
With government funding hard to come by, AI-powered robotics companies have turned to public markets. In August, Unitree, one of China’s largest producers of humanoid robots, went public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange. The company raised nearly $1 billion in its initial public offering, and shares were so oversubscribed that they jumped more than 450 percent on the first day of trading. But although public markets can help fill some of the gap left by shrinking state support, their reach is limited. Only a handful of robotics companies have gone public, and Chinese regulators are making it harder to do so by requiring firms to demonstrate stable revenue and commercial sales before they can list. Regulators are cautious in part because the technology is not yet commercially viable at scale.

articles.title: Why Europe Lost Its Seat at the Iran Nuclear Table? - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Why Europe Lost Its Seat at the Iran Nuclear Table?  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
For most of the past two decades, the Iran nuclear file was where Europe proved it could do geopolitics. Britain, France and Germany opened talks with Tehran in 2003, kept them alive through years of American scepticism, delivered the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action in 2015, and then spent the years after Washington’s 2018 withdrawal trying to keep that agreement breathing. Whatever Europe’s limits as a strategic actor elsewhere, there was one file on which the E3 were the indispensable broker.
That role has now disappeared. When the United States and Israel launched their air war on Iran on 28 February 2026, European capitals declined to join, called for the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened, and then watched as others negotiated the terms of a pause. The memorandum that halted the fighting was brokered by Pakistan, with Europe exercising no influence over the settlement. Today, with US-Iran talks stalled and Secretary of State Marco Rubio accusing Tehran of passing up repeated chances for a nuclear deal, the question about Europe is no longer how it might broker an agreement, but whether it has anything left to bring to one.
The standard explanation is that Europe was distracted, with Ukraine absorbing its attention and budgets. That is true, but incomplete. The deeper problem is that Europe spent its most valuable leverage before the war began, and has since drifted from mediator to co-sponsor of an American pressure campaign whose outcome it does not control.
The lever that was pulled
In August 2025, the E3 triggered the snapback mechanism under UN Security Council Resolution 2231, and previously lifted UN sanctions were reapplied on 27 September 2025. The logic was defensible. The mechanism was due to expire in October 2025, Iran was in serious breach of its commitments, and inspectors had lost track of its highly enriched uranium. Use it or lose it forever.
But snapback was always more valuable as a threat than as an act. Its unique value lay in the fact that it allowed the E3 to restore UN sanctions without exposure to a Russian or Chinese veto, which gave Europe something Washington, having left the deal, no longer had. Once pulled, it could not be pulled again. Europe converted a one-time deterrent into a sanctions regime that Moscow and Beijing openly contest, with China telling the Council that the mechanism contained legal and procedural loopholes, and that Tehran has largely absorbed rather than bowed to.
The cost was not only material. By invoking snapback, the E3 moved from the position of guarantor of a deal to that of a party to pressure against Iran. A broker is useful to both sides because it holds something each wants. After September 2025, Tehran had little reason to see the E3 as anything other than an extension of the Western pressure track. So when war came five months later, Europe’s channel to Tehran was already diminished, and rather than reviving it, Europe left the mediation entirely to others.
From broker to co-sponsor
The clearest sign of where Europe now stands came in Vienna last month. On 9 September 2026, the IAEA Board of Governors voted to refer Iran to the UN Security Council for non-compliance, the first such referral in 20 years. The resolution was sponsored by the United States, Britain, France and Germany, and passed by 23 votes to 3, with 8 abstentions.
On paper, it was a diplomatic success. In practice, it exposed the narrowness of Europe’s position. The referral imposes no new sanctions, and concrete Council action is unlikely, given Russian and Chinese vetoes. Iran’s mission in Vienna seized on the move as evidence that its sponsors no longer believed in snapback. That is a partisan reading, but it raises an awkward question European diplomats have not answered convincingly. If snapback had already returned the Iran file to the Council’s agenda, what was a second referral meant to achieve?
More importantly, the resolution showed that Europe’s Iran diplomacy has become difficult to tell apart from Washington’s. The E3 now act alongside the United States as one bloc of four in Vienna, not as a distinct pole with its own channel to Tehran. That alignment may be politically comfortable, but it surrenders the very quality that once made Europe useful to all parties.
Meanwhile, the substance of the nuclear problem has worsened. The IAEA reported in September that it still cannot verify Iran’s stockpile of 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60 percent, and that Tehran continues to deny inspectors access to more than 20 nuclear sites. A June US-Iran framework that envisaged diluting the highly enriched uranium under IAEA supervision has not been implemented. The programme Europe built its diplomatic identity around is less verifiable today than at any point since the E3 first sat down with Tehran.
Why Europe stayed out
To be fair to European governments, their absence was partly a choice, and not an irrational one. For most capitals, Ukraine remained the overriding priority. The United States has spent months pressing for a Hormuz naval coalition, but European powers have been reluctant to enter a war whose design they had no part in. Early on, European governments also doubted that the strikes were backed by any realistic long-term plan for Iran or the region.
Nor was Europe entirely silent. France maintained direct and indirect contacts with Tehran and floated its own ideas on securing Hormuz once hostilities ended. But individual national channels are not the same as the collective E3 format that once spoke with the weight of the whole continent. Fragmented contacts let each capital protect its own interests; they do not give Europe a seat at the table as a single actor with something to offer.
The difficulty is that strategic restraint without diplomatic presence produced the worst of both outcomes. Europe absorbed the energy consequences of a blockade on a waterway vital to its own energy supply, yet had no hand in shaping the arrangement that might end it. It bore the costs of the war without acquiring a voice in the peace.
What is left
Europe is not without assets, but none of them are glamorous, and all of them require it to accept a narrower role than the one it used to play.
The first is technical. Any durable agreement will rest on verification, and whoever shapes the inspection regime shapes the deal. When the four Western powers table a resolution in Vienna, it has consistently passed. Rather than spending that weight only on censure, Europe could invest it in the unglamorous work of designing how dilution, inventory accounting and site access would actually function under a settlement.
The second is sanctions relief as a currency. Britain, France and Germany have said they are willing to lift certain sanctions under a new nuclear agreement. Washington has signalled that any released Iranian funds would be restricted to buying US food and medicine. Iran’s broader economic reintegration, however, runs through European markets and through the UN sanctions that snapback restored, which Washington cannot unwind on its own.
The third is institutional. The memorandum’s framework envisages that a final agreement would be endorsed by the Security Council, as the 2015 deal was. France and Britain sit on that Council as permanent members. Europe cannot write the deal, but a deal requiring Council endorsement cannot be finalised without it.
These are the levers of a ratifier, not an architect. Using them well would require Europe to decide what it actually wants from the Iran file, whether that is verified non-proliferation, freedom of navigation in Hormuz, or a regional order in which it still has a seat. It would also require Europe to recover enough distance from Washington’s position to be useful to Tehran without becoming an obstacle to Washington.
The broader lesson reaches beyond Iran. Legal mechanisms such as snapback are deterrents whose value lies largely in the possibility that they might be used. Europe treated a lever as a deadline, pulled it, and found that what it gained in legal clarity it lost in diplomatic relevance. In a strategic environment increasingly shaped by force and bilateral bargaining, Europe’s influence will depend less on the frameworks it once authored than on whether it can still bring something the main parties need. On Iran, it still can, but its margin is now very thin.
