articles.summary: Russia Launches Manhunt for Europe’s Top Defense Executives, FT Reports  UNITED24 MediaRussia steps up bid to kill European defence chiefs, spy agencies warn  Financial TimesRussia is targeting heads of defence companies. Europe has already had warning signals  Defence24.comEuropean security agencies warned about Russian sabotage plans  The Brussels TimesRussia steps up assassination attempts targeting defence company executives in Europe, FT says &nb...
articles.full_text:
Russia is reportedly targeting senior executives and key employees of European defense companies for assassination, as Moscow expands covert operations aimed at intimidating arms manufacturers and disrupting military support for Ukraine.
According to the Financial Times on October 11, intelligence officials from five European countries warned that Russian intelligence agencies are increasingly targeting personnel at both major defense manufacturers and smaller companies, particularly those producing drones and military equipment for Ukraine.
European intelligence services have already identified and disrupted several suspected Russian operations, including cases involving surveillance of potential targets near their homes and workplaces.
Officials believe Russia’s military intelligence agency, commonly known as the GRU, is coordinating much of the activity. Russian operatives are reportedly working with organized criminal networks, recruiting local intermediaries, and distributing assignments among individuals operating across different countries.
The use of criminal organizations allows Russian intelligence services to conduct operations through intermediaries while making it more difficult for investigators to establish direct connections to Moscow.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), has increased its engagement with defense companies in response to the threat. Executives and employees have been advised to strengthen security arrangements, including hiring private protection.
BfV President Sinan Selen has warned German lawmakers that Russia is deliberately planning violent attacks against individuals, with organized criminal groups playing an increasingly prominent role in such operations.
Several defense industry executives told the Financial Times that they had increased personal security over the past six months following warnings from intelligence services. Others have introduced additional protective measures when traveling internationally.
The growing security requirements are also creating financial challenges for defense manufacturers. Smaller companies and startups face potentially significant expenses associated with protecting employees, facilities, and sensitive operations.
According to the FT, one defense company relocated its production operations to another part of Western Europe because of threats attributed to Russia.
European intelligence officials believe the reported assassination plots are intended not only to eliminate specific individuals but also to intimidate the wider defense industry.
By making executives and employees fear becoming targets, Moscow reportedly hopes to discourage European manufacturers from supplying weapons, drones, and military technologies to Ukraine.
The Financial Times also reported that some suspected Russian operatives have demonstrated limited operational capabilities, allowing European security services to detect surveillance activities and prevent planned attacks.
The reported threats follow an earlier Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, CEO of German defense manufacturer Rheinmetall. In January 2025, NATO confirmed that US and German intelligence agencies had thwarted the assassination plan, which was reportedly part of a broader campaign targeting European defense industry leaders supplying Ukraine.

articles.title: How Ukraine Could Explode Trump’s ‘Deal With the Devil’ - Newsweek
articles.summary: How Ukraine Could Explode Trump’s ‘Deal With the Devil’  NewsweekWhy Trump is going for Zelenskyy’s jugular  Financial TimesIn the Russia-Ukraine War, Does Trump Know How to Play Cards?  Just SecurityPutin’s war in Ukraine was on life support. Trump has handed him a defibrillator  The IndependentTrump will blame Zelenskyy for losing midterms, diplomat warns  The New Voice of Ukraine
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump likes to think of foreign policy as a business. Allies should earn their keep and adversaries should be made to pay, unless they can make an offer that leaves America better off than it was before.
The man who brought you The Art Of The Deal and a few too many seasons of The Apprentice should really know when he’s the one being taken for a ride.
Vladimir Putin is currently waging a war on Ukraine and threatening Washington’s historical allies across the pond, while the Kremlin’s digital operatives spread fabricated news and attempt to manipulate the American political conversation via extensive disinformation campaigns.
This, according to the White House, should not discount the Russian president from consideration as Washington’s best partner to help resolve America’s fuel crisis.
Trump’s Russian diesel import deal, hashed out over the phone to Moscow last week, is likely to leave Putin better off, Ukraine worse off, and Americans with little to show for it. But Kyiv's recent strikes on Russian data centers suggest it might’ve found another way to make life hard for Putin, and demonstrate why Ukraine, not Russia, could be the more valuable partner for Washington.
Lose-Lose-Win
Trump’s answer to the fuel crisis is not an answer. It’s an act of desperation from which there is only one clear beneficiary.
Following a phone call with Putin on Friday, Trump announced that Russia would supply 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, another 500,000 in November and a million more shortly afterward. To get the diesel moving, the Treasury promptly relaxed sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027 and authorized imports directly into the United States.
There are, unsurprisingly, a few issues here. For starters, Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022, with provisions requiring Moscow to agree to end hostilities and withdraw its forces on terms acceptable to Ukraine before the U.S. president can terminate the ban.
Putin has done nothing of the sort. On the contrary, the Kremlin said he had not even committed to resuming peace negotiations during his phone call with Trump. The president did not consult Congress before striking his bargain, either, and senators from both parties have already demanded the deal be reversed on legal grounds. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer described the agreement as “a deal with the devil.”
Secondly, the deal makes a mockery of Trump’s own demands that European allies stop buying Russian oil, and his repeated threats to punish China and India for keeping the Kremlin’s coffers topped up.
Less than a month ago, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, giving him the tools to further squeeze Russia’s energy profits and impose punitive tariffs on its biggest trading partners. Newsweek labeled this Trump’s latest TACO test, asking to what extent the president would actually use this sanctions sledgehammer. Trump has turned it around and offered Putin the handle to pull him out of a hole.
Of course, Washington might argue that a bit of hypocrisy is worth enduring if Americans can finally catch a break at the pump.
Unfortunately, the numbers are hardly encouraging. America consumes roughly 3.6 million barrels of diesel and other distillate fuels every day. Russia’s initial 300,000-ton delivery amounts to around 2.25 million barrels—barely 15 hours’ worth of American demand, even if every drop reaches the United States. That also assumes Putin can, and will, deliver what he promised.
Ukrainian drone strikes have knocked 3.1 million barrels per day of Russian refining capacity offline, according to S&P Global Energy research. Russia’s diesel exports have collapsed, and analysts expect supply constraints to persist well into 2027.
Ukraine, meanwhile, gets the short end of an already very short stick.
Volodymyr Zelensky previously said he would be willing to halt Kyiv’s deep-strike campaign against Russian refineries—one of Ukraine’s most effective strategies to complicate Putin’s war effort—provided Russia agreed in turn to stop bombing Ukrainian energy facilities.
But Russia’s attacks continued, as did Ukraine’s. And when Zelensky criticized Trump’s diesel deal, the American president lashed out, declaring that it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Kyiv is therefore being forced to choose between sacrificing one of its most effective weapons to stay in the White House’s good graces, or defying a president who controls crucial military and intelligence support. Putin, meanwhile, enjoys sanctions relief and a potentially lucrative export opportunity, without making a meaningful concession in return.
But Ukraine may have just discovered another way to demonstrate its value to the United States—and remind Americans which country is really threatening their interests.
The (Dis)information Age
While Trump was negotiating with Putin, Ukrainian drones were busy making a nuisance of themselves beyond Russia’s refineries.
Between October 8 and 11, three data centers operated by Yandex, Russia’s equivalent to Google, were struck by drones. Yandex’s sprawling digital empire accounts for roughly 70 percent of Russian internet search, provides vital cloud computing and AI services for countless Russian businesses, and boasts 61.5 million monthly users across its taxi, shopping and delivery services.
Russian media published widespread reports of Yandex customers struggling to make payments, order taxis and use other Yandex services amid the strikes, while businesses using Yandex’s cloud computing experienced significant disruptions. The company's shares fell more than 8 percent between October 7 and 9, before the third strike, and it could not say when its damaged facilities would be restored.
Clearly, Ukraine has the capacity to inflict serious damage on the digital infrastructure underpinning Russia’s economy, just as it has done with the energy industry by targeting refineries and the consumer sector by striking the facilities of Russian e-commerce giants. Perhaps Kyiv could take this a step further.
For years, Moscow has invested enormous resources in online operations designed to manipulate political discourse, sow distrust and inflame divisions in Western societies, particularly the United States. American authorities have repeatedly uncovered networks of fake accounts, websites and coordinated propaganda campaigns connected to the Russian state.
In 2024, the U.S. Justice Department disrupted an AI-assisted Russian bot farm involving 968 fictitious social media accounts, which investigators linked to Russia’s FSB intelligence service and state broadcaster RT. That same year, authorities seized 32 internet domains allegedly connected to a Kremlin-directed influence operation targeting American voters and undermining support for Ukraine.
With midterm elections around the corner, Russia’s disinformation machinery is showing no signs of slowing.
In September, researchers at Graphika exposed another Russia-aligned campaign circulating fabricated news reports and manipulated videos attacking American politicians running for office in November, including Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff. The operation even appropriated footage of celebrities including Julia Roberts and Sarah Jessica Parker, alongside fake CNN, BBC and Politico branding, to give its allegations an air of credibility.
Whether these campaigns meaningfully influenced American public opinion is hard to determine, but their purpose is unmistakable. Russia is attempting to manipulate America’s political conversation, including in the weeks before voters go to the polls.
Therein lies a tantalizing opportunity for Kyiv. If Ukrainian intelligence can identify the networks, operators and infrastructure behind Russia’s interference campaigns, and turn Kyiv’s drones on them, Zelensky could deliver exactly what the White House keeps demanding of its allies: a concrete contribution to American security and interests, rather than another request for assistance.
Putin is offering Washington diesel. Ukraine could offer something rather more valuable: a tangible defense of American society and democracy. Then again, perhaps Trump wouldn’t welcome the help; the latest Russia-aligned influence campaign exposed by Graphika was targeting Democrats, not Republicans.
Why would Putin want to do anything to undermine an American president willing to buy his diesel, relax his sanctions and give Ukraine a public telling-off?

articles.title: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports - BBC
articles.summary: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports  BBCWho Are Houthis And Why Are They Attacking Saudi Arabia?  NDTVWhy are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?  The GuardianHow a series of miscalculations restarted Saudi Arabia’s war in Yemen  CNNThe Only Thing the Houthis Have Done Successfully  The Atlantic
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.
"The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.
On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.
The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.
A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.
Explosions were heard again in Riyadh on Monday night, with the Saudi-led military coalition saying a ballistic missile had been intercepted and destroyed.
A Houthi spokesperson said the group had again targeted the airport.
Meanwhile, Qatar Airways has said it will temporarily suspend flights to Riyadh and the north-eastern city of Dammam.
Etihad Airways said it had cancelled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to "regional disruption".
King Khalid airport is expected to remain closed until Saturday.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said early on Tuesday that the Houthis had shot down what he described as a Saudi "reconnaissance drone".
Meanwhile, the official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed "two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Khamis Mushait", in a statement shared on Tuesday.
The WPC Energy Congress opened on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km (6 miles) from Riyadh's airport, which has been attacked four times over the past week.
Last Thursday, three Saudis, including a pilot for the national airline Saudia, were killed in two strikes on an airport facility and an aircraft on the ground.
Another four Saudis, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, one Sudanese and one Indian, were killed in Saturday's missile strike on Terminal 3.
On Sunday, a Pakistani resident was killed when a projectile hit Terminal 4, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was also attacked on Sunday evening, it said, but no casualties were reported.
Later, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces had intercepted a drone in Eastern Province and a missile launched by the Houthis towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait.
Meanwhile, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.
In his inaugural address to the WPC Energy Congress on Monday, Prince Abdul Aziz thanked industry executives and policymakers for attending despite the attacks.
"You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said.
But he also acknowledged that "energy security cannot be taken for granted" and that recent developments had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience".
Prince Abdul Aziz promised that his country would overcome those challenges.
"We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people," he said. "We shall prove it to the world that whatever we are going through we will overcome it."
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".
Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.
UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.
President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.
Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

articles.summary: India Uses Overwhelming Force to Quell Delhi Protests  Drop Site NewsThe Guardian view on Narendra Modi’s gen Z crackdown: he cannot arrest his way out of a democratic crisis | Editorial  The GuardianIndia’s ‘Cockroach’ Leaders Released as Small Protests Go On in Delhi  The New York TimesIndia Locks Down Heart of Capital to Thwart Voter Rights Protest  WSJ‘Not backing down’: What next after India’s crackdown on youth protesters?  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
As a reader-funded independent news outlet, we operate free from the influence of governments, advertisers, and corporate backers. This is essential to our mission: to report on what matters most, beholden only to the truth. In that spirit, we made a commitment to ensure that our journalism is free for everyone, not locked behind a paywall. But that means we rely on the voluntary support of our community of readers. DELHI, India—Indian authorities enforced an unprecedented crackdown on demonstrations across Delhi on Saturday and Sunday, as student groups and citizen networks, including lawyers and doctors organized to provide support for people protesting a massive purge of voter lists. The government deployed over 20,000 police and paramilitary personnel to prevent protestors from gathering in the city, pulling forces from border areas, including Kashmir, into Delhi.
For the past two weeks, protestors across India have been demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, after an investigation by The Indian Express, a prominent daily, revealed that the country’s election commission had deleted more than 130 million people from voter rolls without due process.
The call for large demonstrations on Saturday was made by the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), which in July led widespread protests against the education minister Dharmendra Pradhan for irregularities in nationwide examinations, leading to his resignation. On Saturday, Delhi police detained Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, along with several other leaders of the group, on their airplane when they arrived at the Delhi airport, holding them until Sunday morning.
The mobilization was supposed to be held at the designated protest site of Jantar Mantar, but it was entirely barricaded by the police, and most of central Delhi was under police lockdown.
Many of those who responded to the CJP’s call to action were out on the streets on their way to Jantar Mantar when Dipke and others were detained in the flight. Unable to reach the protest site, they wandered around the city. “Everytime the police stopped us on our way here, we told them we are tourists who are lost, so they let us pass by,” said Shubham Sharma, 22, who was there with his 20-year-old cousin, Harsh.
Multiple journalists were detained, despite wearing their press badges. Lawyers were detained as well, including senior Supreme Court advocate Shadan Farasat, who was carried by his arms and legs to a police station. Overall, police detained over 2,000 protestors on Saturday, reported Reuters. Among those detained was the distinguished welfare economist Jean Drèze, who is originally from Belgium but has lived in India for nearly five decades, working on issues of poverty. “In almost 50 years of being in India, I have never seen such use of force to quell protests,” Drèze told Drop Site from the police station.
Another protestor, 40-year-old Maalvi Mishra said that even as she was entering the lane to get to the protest site, she was told by the police that “Jantar Mantar is not in Delhi,” and that she should go home. “I managed to come here but so many others couldn’t,” she said, as she held up a copy of the constitution in her hands, surrounded by cops and border security forces all around.
As protesters began entering the neighboring areas, police detained anyone who appeared to be heading towards the protest site.
“I reached Delhi from Punjab early in the morning and have been here since,” said Karan Singh, who had travelled alone to attend the protests. “It was incredibly difficult to reach here, I had to walk for almost an hour. The police presence in the area makes it feel like it’s fully a dictatorship,” he said.
Drop Site saw protestors being detained within minutes of chanting slogans, or as soon as they merely came close to the barricaded roads outside Jantar Mantar. It wasn’t just protestors—many were picked up from far beyond the protest premises, from arbitrary spots in the city, without explanation. “I didn’t know anything about the protest, I am in the city for some work with my wife. The police just whisked me away without informing me why,” said Mohammad Rahim, who was detained along with nearly 40 others in front of the New Delhi Railway Station.
In addition to the brute force applied by security forces, members of the right-wing Hindu Raksha Dal (Hindu Protection Force), who mobilized in support of the Narendra Modi government, were seen harassing some protestors. In a video that’s now gone viral, four men were seen attacking a man and a woman, beating them up, with the police not intervening to stop them. The four were arrested on Sunday.
Protests Despite Crackdown
As crackdowns against protestors continued unabated, spontaneous demonstrations erupted in other parts of the city. A popular market for tourists called Dilli Haat suddenly emerged as the go-to spot as left wing student leader Neha Bora announced that as their choice of protest ground. A few hours later, the Safdarjung flyover, an extremely busy overpass in the heart of South Delhi, became another hot spot. The protests, however, could only occur in bursts, as people were being detained within minutes.
“Till the time there is even one person protesting on the street, this movement will continue,” said Bora in a video message on social media. Bora pleaded with supporters to protest wherever the police tried to detain them.
Even as the largely young, Gen Z protestors were being bundled into police buses and vans, some from the older generations came to show solidarity and support.
Hansraj Bhutani, 82, came out into the street with food and water in his bag. “I am here to support the protestors,” he said. “I have lived through the Emergency under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Even then, things weren’t this bad. I am requesting Modi to stop troubling the public like this.”
In Connaught Place, a central market in Delhi, hundreds of protestors trying to make their way to Jantar Mantar were detained. The police presence in the area heavily outnumbered the protestors. The government prohibited the gathering of more than five people in central Delhi.
Many protestors, who had walked in alone, found solidarity with the few others who managed to make it past the barricades.
Papri Das, Pavneet Kaur, and Rosy met each other at the Connaught Place market while heading towards the protest site. “It is disheartening to see how the government is seeking to silence our voices. But what is heartening is that people are still showing up, despite the crackdowns and despite the police brutality,” said Das, 34.
For Kaur, 35, the solidarity she found among each other gave her hope that this movement could be successful. “We just realized that the three of us belong to different religions. I am Sikh, Papri is Hindu, and Rosy is Muslim. This is exactly what the government fears—people becoming united to fight its tyranny,” she said.
Not far from Connaught Place, police entered a Sikh temple, the Gurudwara Bangla Sahib, and detained people en masse. “I witnessed at least a dozen people being brutalized while the Delhi police tried to detain them. One 75-year-old woman was brutalized by the police so badly, one of her fingers was dangling off, we had to get her a plastic surgery,” said a doctor who was offering medical relief to the injured inside the Gurudwara and did not want to be named out of fear of retaliation.
He said that the police entered the temple premises in their boots and without wearing a head scarf—as required of men entering Sikh places of worship. “Most people were injured due to the police twisting their fingers while trying to detain them. I saw a lot of pinching and nail marks on injured protestors. They are not using batons, but using these other means to brutalize protestors,” he said.
The protests continued on Sunday, with spontaneous marches emerging in Connaught Place multiple times throughout the day and the police detaining hundreds of protestors. “I have been detained almost every day since October 2. I will continue to protest this regime and I will continue to show up on protest sites every day, there is no fear anymore,” one protester told Drop Site through a window of a police bus.
Support Networks
In response to the July protests, a citizen-led volunteer group began to take shape. The group, which calls itself the Protest Support Initiative, has multiple wings, each catering to a different aspect of providing aid and support, with about 150 volunteers. One wing is in charge of driving people home after they are let go from their detention centers, often in far-flung places. Another, led by doctors, is in charge of providing first-aid. There’s also a wing of therapists who help people who’ve undergone trauma during the detention or during confrontation with the police.
For Meghnad, a popular journalist and content creator, forming the group seemed like the most natural thing to do. “No one else was doing it, but someone had to. So might as well be us,” he said. “Eighteen year olds would come up to me asking how do we get home after the police leave us in random parts of the city after detention, I had to help them. I also realized many of these young protesters come from extremely repressive environments at home. They’ve found a space to express themselves through these protests, so we have to be there for them.” 
Until October 9, the group had 20 people who had volunteered to drive detainees home. After the October 10 protests, that number has risen to 93. But along with all the support, they now also face the scrutiny and intimidation that comes from the authorities. “Three people were following me throughout the protests on 10th. articles.title: Houthi assault on Saudi airports strikes at MBS’s economic vision - Financial Times
articles.summary: Houthi assault on Saudi airports strikes at MBS’s economic vision  Financial TimesSaudi Arabia's Riyadh airport hit by second Houthi strike in two days  BBCFresh concerns over 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia after missile strikes in Riyadh  The GuardianIran war updates: Saudi downs Houthi missiles during ongoing deadly attacks  Al JazeeraSaudi warning system stayed silent before deadly airport attacks  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Dozens of passengers stand in line as they prepare to board a flight to Jeddah in western Saudi Arabia, many of them pilgrims en route to Mecca. As one, dressed in simple white garb, leans to pick up his bag from the floor, the camera shakes violently and suddenly. A white flash fills the screen as debris falls from the ceiling, and people run for safety.
The scene, captured in dramatic CCTV footage, marks the moment of a deadly Houthi missile attack on Saturday, one of hundreds launched by the Iran-backed militant group across the kingdom since the years-long conflict reignited in July.
That it happened in Riyadh’s main international airport — killing 13 people and injuring over 300 — underscores the dramatic escalation of the Iran-backed rebels’ campaign, one that has now hit at the heart of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 programme to transform Saudi Arabia into a regional finance and events centre.
Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport is central to these ambitions, with the government planning a major expansion as it prepares to host global events including Expo 2030 and the Fifa World Cup in 2034. It also serves as the home base of Riyadh Air, a new airline backed by the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund that aims to turn the city into a transport hub competing with Dubai and Doha.
But the airport, which has been hit five times since Wednesday, will now be closed until at least Friday, according to a notice given to airlines. Attacks on other airports including in Dammam and the south-west, as well as disruptions in Jeddah — the largest by traffic — have forced the cancellation of thousands of more flights.
“There is little question that the attacks by the Houthis on Saudi airports . . . were designed to damage the kingdom’s global standing while crippling an essential part of Vision 2030,” said Sean Foley, professor of Middle East history at Middle Tennessee State University.
They have come during a busy period in Saudi Arabia’s business calendar. The kingdom is preparing to host later this month the Future Investment Initiative event, its flagship economic conference that typically attracts Wall Street executives, global investors and bankers, while the World Petroleum Council’s energy congress began on Sunday in Riyadh.
The chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell and BP were all expected to attend the WPC congress but withdrew following the Houthi attacks, the FT reported on Sunday.
Other events were also affected. The organisers of Misk Global Forum — an annual conference organised by an NGO affiliated with the crown prince — said on Monday they were cancelling their event scheduled for next month.
A private equity firm also cancelled a planned investor day this week in Riyadh after losing most of its speakers. “Even the ones in Saudi have to attend to bigger problems,” the firm’s chief executive said.
Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s energy minister, struck a defiant tone at the WPC congress on Monday, telling the audience — which included fewer attendees in western-style clothing than would ordinarily be expected at such an event — that “the word fear in the Saudi dictionary does not exist”.
But with Riyadh’s airport closed for days, many of the energy officials and other business executives currently in the capital could be forced to take a land route to neighbouring Gulf states such as Bahrain or Qatar to catch flights back home.
And experts say the repeated failure of Saudi air defences to protect airports risks doing longer-term damage to the kingdom’s image and its ability to attract foreign investors and tourists, both vital for the success of the crown prince’s economic plans.
Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House, said the targeting of airports was designed to inflict maximum damage on the kingdom’s economic infrastructure and reputation.
“This is a huge part of the Houthis’ calculation,” he said. “Saudi Arabia has something to lose and they do not. It is the economy where they feel they can cause the most harm.”
The conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis first began more than a decade ago, after the kingdom intervened in Yemen’s civil war to restore the internationally recognised government against the Iran-backed militants.
The intervention came just months before Prince Mohammed unveiled his plan to transform the Saudi economy by diversifying away from oil revenues, removing some social restrictions in the conservative kingdom and developing new sectors such as tourism, logistics and technology.
Riyadh soon became bogged down in a hugely costly campaign in Yemen, before a fragile truce with the Houthis in 2022 seemed to provide the regional stability needed for the kingdom to forge ahead with Prince Mohammed’s plans.
But while Saudi Arabia was less hard hit than some neighbours like the United Arab Emirates by Iranian attacks following the start of the US and Israeli war against Tehran earlier this year, the truce with the Houthis ultimately collapsed over the summer.
The rebels declared a maritime blockade against Saudi ships passing through strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which had become a vital outlet for Saudi oil after the US-Iran war in effect closed the Strait of Hormuz.
They also fired waves of missiles and drones at energy facilities in Saudi Arabia’s southern provinces, threatening the kingdom’s export revenues and roiling global energy markets.
After the Saudi-backed Yemeni government this month announced a new offensive against the Houthis, the group responded by escalating its targeting of Saudi airports, first in the kingdom’s south-west and then Riyadh itself.
An adviser to the Saudi government acknowledged that the airport attacks will hurt foreign investment and tourism in what was already a turbulent year. “Tourism is the first thing hit in a big way,” he said. While it won’t stop religious tourism, “it will stop high-income travel. Investments will get hit. It was already slower this year.”
“Investors will ask: Is there going to be demand?” the adviser added. “Is the facility safe? If you’re an energy investor, you were already spooked.”
Haytham Linjawi, an assistant professor of political science at King Abdulaziz University in Jeddah, argued that Saudi Arabia’s strong global relations and the reforms it implemented as part of Vision 2030 are factors that outweigh the security incidents.
“Travel disruptions are an immediate logistical consideration for organisers,” he said, “but so far they do not appear to alter the underlying investment in upcoming conferences,” with Saudi Arabia continuing to build hotels, venues and expand airports.
But Kristin Smith Diwan, a senior resident scholar at the Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington, said that “as long as the airports are under attack and unsafe, people will not come”.
“You can’t build a globally integrated economy when you can’t protect your airports,” she said. “If security can be restored, attitudes will change. But today that doesn’t seem fully under Riyadh’s control.”

"Worse, it would be a major dereliction of duty" for the government to "turn away" from exploring options for a closer relationship with the European Union, he continued, adding that his "immediate priority" was to land a "successful outcome at the summit," which is scheduled for 20 November.

The PM told an audience at the Labour Party's annual conference in Liverpool last month that Brexit had "done more harm than good" and that the UK needed a clear strategy on its long-term relationship with Brussels.

RAF Fairford incident
Elsewhere in his speech, Burnham said an incident at a UK airbase in September was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as he warned that Britain "will not tolerate these threats."
On 27 September, five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwest England, on suspicion of explosives offensives before being further arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act. They were later released on police bail.
Police later arrested another man, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, in London on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts related to the incident. A 22-year-old British man was then arrested on 6 October, also in London and on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts. Both were released on police bail.
According to UK Counter Terrorism Policing, all seven men remain on police bail as specialist teams "continue to pursue all lines of enquiry."
RAF Fairford is home to the US Air Force's 501st Combat Support Wing headquarters and the 420th Air Base squadron. It has also served as the USAF Global Strike Command's preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe.
In July, the IRGC said it was aware that the base was being used by US bombers as part of Washington's military operations against Iran and warned the UK that "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces."
The US has now withdrawn its bombers from Fairford.

articles.summary: NAZA: Netanyahu orders identification and prosecution of film’s interviewees  The GuardianNetanyahu demands probe into sources for award-winning Gaza film NAZA  Al JazeeraJames Wilson on the “vituperative, aggressive” Israeli backlash to ‘NAZA’ and class privilege in UK film  Screen DailyGaza Doc ‘NAZA’ Surpasses $500K Without Distributor After Sparking Protests  The Hollywood ReporterNetanyahu seeks criminal charges for NAZA participants  Middle...

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the country’s attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of soldiers and officers interviewed in the investigative documentary NAZA and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.
The award-winning documentary, directed by the Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza. The film is in cinemas, including in the UK and the US, and will be shown in more than 50 countries.
In a letter addressed to the attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, the IDF chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, and the Shin Bet head, David Zini, the Israeli prime minister demanded they “act urgently to uncover the identity of all those who are involved or appear in the libel film”.
Netanyahu also called for “the opening of a criminal investigation and prosecution for serious information security offences, criminal defamation, and harming Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.
NAZA premiered last month at the Venice international film festival, where it won the special jury prize after receiving the longest ovation in the event’s history. It takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate how many civilians it expects to be killed in an airstrike.
The Israeli government has fiercely attacked Abraham and Szor, threatening to strip them of their citizenship and accusing them of treason. Government supporters have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s parents’ home in Savyon, chanting: “Death sentence to traitors.”
Zamir denounced the film as an “attack on the state of Israel”, accusing it of spreading “lies and blood libels”. He had earlier ordered military and legal officials to identify the soldiers featured and examine possible legal action against them. However, the military advocate general, Itai Ofir, said criminal prosecution would require evidence of security violations or disclosure of classified material, although disciplinary measures remained possible.
The protection of journalistic sources is a cornerstone of press freedom under international human rights standards and disclosure orders are permitted only under stringent conditions.
Ricardo Gutiérrez, the general secretary of the European Federation of Journalists, representing over 320,000 journalists, said: “These threats constitute a blatant act of intimidation against journalists who have simply been doing their job, in strict accordance with ethical standards and in the public interest. I am not surprised by this outburst, which confirms that this regime is prepared to do anything to cover up its crimes against humanity and the ongoing genocide in Gaza.”
A Guardian spokesperson said: “After first threatening to strip NAZA’s directors of their Israeli citizenship, the Israeli government is now calling for an investigation into their journalistic sources. These moves are all attempts to distract from the urgent questions the film asks about the mass killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Journalists should be free to pursue public interest investigations without threats or harassment.”
NAZA builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian between 2023 and 2025. Earlier this month, a Guardian spokesperson said the “process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.”
In the past three years the team behind the film has “interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes”, the Guardian spokesperson added.
In recent days, the Israeli government has promoted an online film project that mimics the style of NAZA, in an attempt to challenge the real film’s findings. Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who made NAZA: The Real Story, described it as an “offensive move” intended to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.
Film industry heavyweights across the globe, including the heads of the Locarno film festival, have expressed solidarity with Abraham and Szor, saying they stood “firmly in support of film-makers’ rights to pursue difficult and urgent subjects without fear of reprisal”.

articles.title: Trump’s Russian Diesel Debacle Risks Backfiring - The Moscow Times
articles.summary: Trump’s Russian Diesel Debacle Risks Backfiring  The Moscow TimesTrump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia  BBCUkraine war briefing: Russian diesel exports could return to past levels after Trump deal, Moscow claims  The GuardianTrump turns on Europe after Putin deal  The TelegraphRussia deal, execution plans and deportations tell a defining tale about Trump and power  CNN
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump’s announcement on Oct. 9 that the United States would begin importing Russian diesel has roiled transatlantic relations. Such abrupt and dizzying shifts have been a consistent feature of Trump’s war diplomacy.
To assess its significance, we must distinguish the genuinely new from the wearily familiar. Since there is less to this policy than meets the eye, it is unlikely to have any real impact on the course of the war. Its few novel aspects will merely compound failure with ignominy.
This latest initiative resembles earlier Trumpian forays in three ways.
First, it restores Trump’s natural preference for Russia. Despite taking occasional steps that displeased Moscow, such as sanctioning its two biggest oil companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, Trump always returns to his default setting of rewarding Russia and pressuring Ukraine. Since the fighting can only stop if Moscow is decisively constrained from achieving its war aims, such a policy pursues the opposite of what is needed to end the war. It thus cannot succeed in its strategic goal.
Second, Trump’s main goal is to restore economic ties with Russia and, above all, to make new energy deals. Moscow has repeatedly dangled the carrots of huge investment proposals to American negotiators. While Trump’s latest move concerns energy trade, not investment, even this is not new. From March to June this year, the U.S. granted a temporary license allowing Russia to ship crude and oil products to mitigate the supply shock caused by the war with Iran.
Third, in importing Russian fuel without a quid pro quo, the White House is not striking a deal but making a unilateral concession to Moscow that weakens its negotiating position. Again, this is not new. In 2025, America abandoned earlier positions, notably by dropping the demand on Russia for an immediate ceasefire and the threat of new sanctions. In doing so, it surrendered its leverage and put its own objectives further out of reach. Now, it is repeating this error.
So what is new and consequential about the diesel deal? First, it is driven not by the prospect of lucrative deals for those around the White House, but by the urgent political need to reduce domestic fuel prices before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.
Unlike the temporary waiver in March, which allowed more Russian oil onto the world market, the new volumes will be shipped specifically to the U.S. For this reason, it may be found illegal. A bipartisan group of senators has already declared that the trade would violate the 2022 ban on Russian energy imports and has called for the administration to “immediately reverse course.” The trade also cuts directly across the Lindsey Graham Act, passed with overwhelming congressional support last month, which included provisions to punish major importers of Russian oil.
Second, even in its own terms, the deal may fail. The modest volumes are too small to have any significant effect on prices at the pump and will likely arrive too late for the midterms.
Moreover, Russia may not even be able to deliver them. While it could make use of the temporary waiver Washington granted earlier this year to sell more oil products, Ukrainian attacks on its refineries caused exports to collapse in June. Russia imposed an export ban in July to stem and secure its own supply, but has now lifted it to export to the U.S. But its ability to do so will depend on the perilous security of its energy infrastructure.
All this lays bare the central contradiction in Trump’s position. On the one hand, he attributes the global fuel shortage to Ukraine’s attacks on Russian facilities when his own war against Iran is primarily responsible for the worldwide fuel deficit. On the other hand, he claims that supplies from Russia can meet the shortages that its absence from the market has created.
Third, America has reportedly threatened to cut off Ukraine’s access to intelligence and the PURL program if it continues to target Russian refineries. We have been here before, too. Washington suspended such support for brief periods several times in 2025, most severely in March, and issued similar threats last November to try to compel Zelensky to accept the administration’s 28-point peace plan. These cut-offs lasted only a few days, but hindered Ukraine’s operations.
What is new is the prospect of a longer, perhaps permanent, cut-off from all assistance that would be harmful to Kyiv, but not fatal. Ukraine has developed its own long-range strike weapons and Europe can provide some intelligence. The most serious consequence would be the loss of critically needed Patriot interceptors, 95% of which are obtained for Ukraine through PURL.
But America’s defense industry would suffer too. It would lose not only billions of dollars in weapons sales paid by Europe and delivered to Ukraine, but potentially also Kyiv’s cooperation as a unique and valuable source of technology and data. These losses would far outweigh any impact of a small, brief fall in domestic fuel prices.
In short, much about the diesel deal is a repeat of past efforts. Since it shares their flaws, it will share their failure.
But it adds contradictions of its own: trivial volumes of fuel that may not even arrive and are likely illegal if they do; threats that, if carried out, would hurt America’s national security.
Fresh absurdities appear every day. In its dealings with Russia, the administration has reportedly tried to offer assets, frozen in Europe, that it does not control; has proposed reviving the Nord Stream gas pipeline, a move that would require Europe’s consent; and has announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that neither country was aware of. This is a policy approaching total incoherence.
It was said of the Bourbon dynasty that it learned nothing and forgot nothing. History may record of this White House that, on its Russia policy at least, it learned nothing and understood nothing. Other countries have learned, to their cost, the lessons that await. When policy is driven by venal ineptitude rather than a judicious understanding of the national interest, the result is a masterclass in strategic failure.

articles.title: Super El Nino could make 2026 record hottest year: climate monitor - Yahoo
articles.summary: Super El Nino could make 2026 record hottest year: climate monitor  YahooSurface air temperature for September 2026  Copernicus Climate ChangeSeptember 2026: 2nd-hottest September for Earth, hottest for the U.S.  Yale Climate ConnectionsSeptember 2026 was the third-warmest September for Europe  https://eu-space.europa.eu/Crossing Paris climate target 'only a matter of time'  aapnews.aap.com.au
articles.full_text:
An intensifying El Nino pattern set an all-time temperature high in a key Pacific zone in September and could help make this year the hottest globally on record, the director of the EU's climate monitor said Monday.
Global forecasters have been warning for months that this El Nino would likely become the strongest ever observed and the latest record has tumbled even before the episode's expected peak later this year.
The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino temporarily raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate man-made global warming.
The Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures in a tell-tale El Nino monitoring region of the Pacific, known as Nino3.4, had reached an "all-time high" of 29.70C last month.
This exceeded the peak temperatures of previously strong El Nino events of 1982/1983, 1997/1998 and 2015/2016, the EU monitor said.
This year's El Nino, which emerged in June, is "very exceptional" but it is too early to say whether it is the strongest ever observed, Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo told AFP.
As climate change raises ocean temperatures, it can make recent El Nino events appear stronger than past ones, complicating historical comparisons.
Copernicus said it had adopted a new index, which accounts for the warming of tropical oceans, that suggested the current event is not yet stronger than past ones.
"It's a very large event even in that metric," Buontempo said. "This very large event today is happening in a much warmer climate."
Not all forecasters use the same scale to interpret El Nino.
On Friday, Japan's weather agency said that El Nino conditions had reached their "strongest intensity on record".
- Record ocean temperatures -
As El Nino gathers strength, global average sea surface temperatures hit a record 21.05C for September, topping the previous high of 20.92C for the same month in 2023, according to Copernicus.
Experts have warned that this El Nino, combined with human-induced climate change, could make 2027 the hottest year on record as heat stored in the Pacific is released into the atmosphere.
The weather phenomenon, which typically occurs every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months, can drive world temperatures higher the year after its peak.
But Buontempo said even 2026 could wind up a record breaker as this El Nino builds toward its peak.
"If we follow the the pattern we have seen in the past, we may have a record-breaking 2026, followed by a record-breaking 2027," he told AFP.
After a record-breaking August, the world experienced its second hottest September ever observed, with surface air temperatures averaging 16.27C, the EU service said.
September was 1.63C hotter than the pre-industrial average, a period defined as 1850-1900. It was the second consecutive month that temperature rises exceeded 1.5C.
Buontempo said temperatures would probably remain 1.5C above normal into early next year
The last El Nino event helped make 2024 the hottest year on record after a series of months of temperatures exceeding 1.5C, he said.
But while El Nino plays a role, "the ultimate cause of the rise and the exceedance of 1.5C are anthropogenic emissions of greenhouse gases," Buontempo said.
Nations agreed at the 2015 UN climate talks in Paris to keep global warming "well below" 2C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5C, in order to limit the effects of climate change.
But the United Nations declared in September that the long-term 1.5C target would be missed in a matter of years.
Scientists say it is crucial to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels to limit the period of "overshoot" above 1.5C and bring temperatures back down as quickly as possible.

Forget sleepmaxxing and cold plunging: smoking is the new lifestyle flex among AI researchers.
At least, that's according to Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar, who said some AI researchers are taking up smoking to signal their belief that AI will eventually cure cancer.
"So many AI researchers have started smoking as a way of signaling to other researchers how much they believe in AI," Sankar said in an interview on CBS News' "Face the Nation" on Sunday.
The logic, he said, is: "I believe so much in AI that it's going to cure cancer. So I'm showing you my chips are all in."
Sankar did not name any researchers or provide evidence for the claim. Smoking remains a major cause of preventable illness and death, and no AI breakthrough has eliminated the health risks associated with cigarettes.
But the Palantir executive's remarks echo a countercurrent already visible in parts of the tech industry.
As Business Insider's Henry Chandonnet reported last month, a small group of founders, engineers, and investors has embraced cigarettes in a sector otherwise known for optimizing their health with cold plunges, sleep tracking, and peptide treatments.
For some of them, a cigarette break is an opportunity to meet people and network. For others, it's a way to come across as more relaxed and less polished than the typical startup founder.
And some AI believers expect the technology to make smoking-related health risks a thing of the past.
"By the time you do get lung cancer, our AI robots are supposed to have cured that," Avi Schiffmann, the founder of AI wearable startup Friend, previously told Business Insider.
'The machine god of AGI'
In the CBS News interview, Sankar raised the smoking anecdote while criticizing what he called Silicon Valley's "mass psychosis" and "social delusion" around AI.
He has been outspoken in his criticism of AI safety advocates, whom he accused in the interview of treating artificial general intelligence as a "machine god."
Invoking philosopher Blaise Pascal's idea that humans have a "God-shaped hole" in their hearts, Sankar said that some people in Silicon Valley have placed quasi-religious faith in AGI.
"I think it's important to understand that many of these folks in Silicon Valley who are building this technology have filled that hole with the machine god of AGI," Sankar said.

German foreign Minister Johann Wadephul described a new raft of punitive measures against Russia as an "unprecedented sanction blow" to President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine.
"We are making it harder for Putin to continue his war of aggression in violation of international law, and his cynical attempt to wear down Ukraine's civilian population through murderous bombing campaigns," Wadephul said on Monday as EU foreign ministers met in Luxembourg to finalize the sanctions package.
Who do the sanctions target?
It targets some 1,600 individuals and businesses related to Russia's war effort, and another 77 people and groups related to what the EU sees as illegal elections in occupied Ukrainian terrorities.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a post on X that this was "the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war...More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles."
"We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians," she added.
Although he could not attend the Luxembourg meeting due to a party conference in Berlin, Wadephul said: "The message is clear: Russia cannot and will not win this war."
However, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appeared to imply that sanctions need to go even further as the conflict was set to enter its fifth bitter winter.
"This is the moment when the entire West...should show Russia and Putin that it is ready to pursue a policy of containing Russia by even more decisive means," he told the Warsaw Security Forum, referring to EU sanctions. "That is why I will go to Brussels to persuade all our European partners to seriously consider increasing sanctions against Russia.
What is the latest development in the war?
Russian forces have repeatedly stepped up attacks on Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure every autumn since its invasion, hoping to cripple heating and other necessary utilitiesahead of winter.
US President Donald Trump declared that there was an "energy ceasefire" in place between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend. However, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had no idea what Trump was referring to and that Russia had continued to target energy facilities unabated.

articles.title: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles, adding to streak of weapons tests - AP News
articles.summary: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles, adding to streak of weapons tests  AP NewsNorth Korea test-fires suspected ballistic missiles, Japan says  ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and VideosNorth Korea continues streak of weapons tests with multiple ballistic missile launches  CBS NewsNorth Korea fires missiles days after South Korea's hypersonic test  ReutersNorth Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korea on Monday fired multiple ballistic missiles toward its eastern waters, South Korea’s military said, adding to a recent streak of weapons demonstrations that has heightened tensions during a prolonged freeze in diplomacy.
Jang Do-young, spokesperson of South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, said missiles of various types were fired from an area around the North Korean capital of Pyongyang, where the country’s main airport has been a major launch site in recent years.
Jang said one of the missiles flew more than 900 kilometers (559 miles) before falling into the sea but didn’t comment on the flight details of the other weapons. The joint chiefs didn’t specify how many missiles it detected.
Japan’s Deputy Defense Minister Takashi Koyari said Japan detected at least two missiles launched 17 minutes apart and that the weapons landed in waters outside of its exclusive economic zone. Koyari said the first missile flew about 220 kilometers (137 miles) and the second more than 910 kilometers (565 miles), following an “irregular” flight path, a term Japanese officials have previously used to describe hypersonic weapons. There were no reports of damage to aircraft or vessels, he said.
While maintaining a hard line toward Seoul, North Korea has been ramping up weapons testing as it seeks to expand its arsenal of nuclear-capable systems, including an Oct. 3 test of what the North described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile designed to evade missile defenses in South Korea and Japan.
North Korea has also conducted other missile tests and live-fire drills and commissioned a new warship as leader Kim Jong Un continues to flaunt his nuclear weapons program while rejecting U.S. and South Korean offers to resume long-stalled diplomacy.
The latest launch came days after South Korea on Friday flight-tested its own domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defense systems, which President Lee Jae Myung described as critical in strengthening the South’s conventional defense capabilities. Without directly addressing the growing threat from North Korea, Lee’s office said the hypersonic weapon, once fully developed, would enhance South Korea’s ability to strike key targets by surprise in the “Korean Peninsula theater of operations.”
Jang, the South Korean military official, said the latest North Korean launches likely were intended to advance the country’s missile technologies while also serving as a possible response to South Korea’s hypersonic test.
The South’s presidential national security office called for North Korea to “immediately cease” its repeated ballistic launches, which violate U.N. Security Council resolutions against the North and “do not help manage the current situation on the Korean Peninsula.” Koyari said Japan lodged a protest to North Korea through their embassies in Beijing.
Tensions were further worsened after three South Korean soldiers were injured in land mine explosions last month near the heavily armed inter-Korean border. The South’s military and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded the blasts were caused by devices planted by North Korea, which has denied responsibility and ridiculed the South’s demands for an apology.
Kim in recent years has halted all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and described the neighbor as a permanent enemy during a prolonged stalemate in larger nuclear negotiations with Washington. He has so far rebuffed U.S. President Donald Trump’s calls to revive their diplomacy, which broke down in 2019, with his government demanding that Washington abandon its “hostile” policy toward Pyongyang and drop demands for North Korea’s denuclearization as a precondition for talks.
___
AP writer Mari Yamaguchi contributed from Tokyo.

articles.title: Trump turns the screws on Kyiv as EU budget talks hit a wall - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Trump turns the screws on Kyiv as EU budget talks hit a wall  Euronews.comAnalysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections  BBCTrump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes  Al JazeeraZelenskyy vows to retaliate if Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continue  The GuardianWhy Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire  BBC
articles.full_text:
Good morning. It’s Monday. I’m Mared Gwyn. Today: Europe braces as Trump turns up the heat on Zelenskyy, and Ireland’s EU budget compromise falls dead on arrival.
Kyiv under pressure: For Ukraine, the past few days have brought back the distinct taste of the Oval Office showdown: public pressure on President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, accusations that Ukraine is obstructing peace and a growing fear (again) that the aim is not compromise, let alone a just peace, but to force Ukraine to surrender, our correspondent Sasha Vakulina writes this morning.
Blindsided: US President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire on attacks against energy infrastructure. There was just one rather significant problem: at least one of those parties appeared unaware of the agreement.
“If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins,” Zelenskyy said in response. Ukraine, he added, was ready.
It was not entirely clear Moscow got the memo either, Sasha explains.After Trump’s announcement, Russia struck a thermal power plant in Kharkiv, before targeting several other power plants overnight. And that was only Sunday.
Diesel deal rattles Europeans: On Friday, Trump had also announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports, without informing Ukrainian or European negotiators who were in Miami for talks. It’s seen as an effort to bring down soaring diesel and gasoline prices, a major issue for American voters, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Zelenskyy did not mince his words, branding the deal “weak” and warning it would hand Putin “billions” more to wage war. Trump told him he “better damn well stop” striking Russian refineries, before taking it further and saying Ukraine needed a “new leader”. Putin’s leadership, notably, did not come up for discussion.
Rallying around Zelenskyy: There is another irony for Trump: publicly berating Zelenskyy has hardly proven an effective way of weakening him at home - quite the opposite. EU leaders have also been rallying behind the Ukrainian leader – and Zelenskyy is now expected to join leaders when they gather for a summit in Brussels this Thursday and Friday, sources have told Euronews.
Hard reckoning: News of the Trump-Putin diesel deal and the subsequent energy ceasefire is also set to dominate the conversation today in Brussels and Luxembourg, where foreign ministers are gathering, Jorge Liboreiro writes.
Once again, the EU finds itself scrambling to close ranks behind Zelenskyy and push back, with calculated criticism, against Trump’s Russian-friendly diplomacy.
The US Treasury’s sanctions waiver to enable the diesel sales, set to last until April 2027, has particularly enraged Europeans, who see their own sanctions regime undermined by Trump’s out-of-the-blue decisions. It must be noted that the majority of vessels that Russia uses to trade its refined oil products are subject to the G7 price cap ($100 per barrel).
Foreign ministers will today make clear their pressure campaign on Moscow will continue unabated by formally blacklisting more than 1,600 people and companies accused of enabling the war, a record number in one go.
“We are of course continuing our path,” Kallas said on sanctions upon arriving in Luxembourg this morning. “Our message is clear. If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia, and we would call on the US to put the sanctions in place so we can finish this war,” she added.
More is needed: Russia’s all-out escalation has forced EU officials and diplomats to admit that their multibillion-euro support for Ukraine will fall short next year. But there are no easy solutions, Jorge writes in his in-depth analysis.
Warsaw watches: The mounting tensions have also raised the stakes of the Warsaw Security Conference kicking off this morning, with President Zelenskyy expected to address delegates from Kyiv in around an hour.
Our chief EU editor Maria Tadeo, on the ground in the Polish capital, reports that security is tight and the mood tense after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sunday that a man had been arrested on suspicion of plotting to assassinate him and his defence minister. More from our Warsaw colleagues.
Dead on arrival: Meanwhile, a new pitch to trim down the EU’s next long-term budget – known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) – tabled by Ireland over the weekend has been met with immediate pushback from the so-called frugal countries, which are demanding a much smaller spending pot.
“The size of the new proposal is not a basis for agreement. The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the brunt of financing it,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a statement on Saturday.
Dutch directness: Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen was even more blunt. “The Netherlands cannot accept this proposal. At this rate, there will be no deal by the end of the year,” he said in a statement. Sweden also rejected the proposal, insisting that the “overall volume” needs to come down.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, on Saturday pitched €141 billion in cuts to the previous proposal in an attempt to appease the frugals. The country’s EU affairs minister, Thomas Byrne, described the proposal as a “compromise designed to act as a catalyst” for wrapping up negotiations by the end of this year – a prospect that now looks increasingly remote.
Crunch time: EU leaders are set to tackle the budget issue when they gather for talks in Brussels on Thursday and Friday – and European Council President António Costa is pushing for a swift compromise. There has been a political push to wrap up the budget negotiations before the end of 2026 to prevent talks from being torpedoed by elections in major EU economies including France, Italy and Poland next year. My colleague Luca Bertuzzi has more.
Oil prices tumble as stocks rise after Trump touts 'energy ceasefire'
Most stock markets rose early Monday as oil prices tumbled after US President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which offset a fresh wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, my colleague Angela Barnes reports.
Both main crude contracts sank more than 1% following the announcement, reversing an initial spike that came in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia at the weekend.
At least a dozen people were killed at Riyadh's international airport Saturday - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil for more than a decade - and another one died following a second strike on Sunday.
The Iran-backed group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the past 24 hours and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom's transit hubs, calling them "a theatre of operations for our forces".
"The market is no longer paying full geopolitical premium on every headline, and that is probably the most useful signal in the morning price action," wrote SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes.
He added: "The physical market remains tight enough to keep Brent above $100, but futures are refusing to treat every new escalation as the start of another straight-line inflation shock."
Angela hasthe details.
More from our newsrooms
Tens of thousands urge EU for climate action at Brussels demonstration. Ahead of a major UN summit, thousands of protesters marched through the streets of Brussels demanding greater action to combat climate change. Euronews’ Evelyn Ann-Marie Dom was on the ground and spoke to protesters and organisers.
Macron's popularity hits lowest level since 2017 as Bardella and Le Pen also lose ground. Some 82% of French people now disapprove of the French President, while the far-right National Rally’s Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella’s ratings were also weakened by Mediapart's revelations about antisemitic texts attributed to Bardella. Alexander Kazakevich hasmore.
North Korea fires 'several ballistic missiles' into Sea of Japan, Seoul's military says. North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles off its east coast, Seoul's military said on Monday, after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border that divides both countries. Gavin Blackburn hasthe details.
We're also keeping an eye on
- Warsaw Security Conference kicks off. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to give the opening address from Kyiv. Speakers include Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and European Commissioner for Defence, Andrius Kubilius.
- EU foreign affairs and environment ministers gather for talks in Luxembourg.
- European Commission Vice-Presidents Stéphane Séjourné and Roxana Mînzatu to address the European Parliament’s employment committee.
That’s it for today. Sasha Vakulina, Jorge Liboreiro and Luca Bertuzzi contributed to this newsletter.

articles.title: Two Ships Struck by Drones in the Black Sea, Radev to Hold Talks with Russian Ambassador and NATO Secretary General - BGNES

articles.full_text:
Two merchant vessels were struck in separate incidents in the Black Sea overnight, according to information provided for the emergency meeting of the Security Council under the Council of Ministers, a BGNES reporter reported.
The Maltese-flagged cargo ship CHELSEA 3 was attacked by three aerial drones approximately 18 nautical miles east of Byala. All 15 crew members were evacuated and transported to Varna. According to preliminary information, five seafarers received medical attention for minor injuries. Another vessel sank approximately 17 nautical miles east of Krapets, with one crew member reported rescued so far. Prime Minister Rumen Radev announced that he would invite Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova for talks and would also speak with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. According to Radev, there is currently insufficient conclusive evidence to establish the origin of the drones used.
Evacuation of the CHELSEA 3 Crew
The distress signal from the vessel was received at 01:30. According to information provided by the crew, the vessel was attacked by three aerial drones that struck its deck and side. The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Varna launched an emergency search and rescue operation, while a Border Police team evacuated all 15 people on board—seven Ukrainian and eight Azerbaijani nationals.
The CHELSEA 3 sails under the Maltese flag, is registered in Odesa and, according to the information provided, is Ukrainian-owned. The crew was transported to the Port of Varna, where five seafarers received medical attention for minor injuries.
Earlier reports on the incident cited a distance of approximately 14–15 nautical miles east of Byala and reported a different number of injured persons. The information provided on the government's response gives the distance as approximately 18 nautical miles and states that 15 people were evacuated. There is insufficient information to conclusively reconcile all the discrepancies in the initial reports.
Second Vessel Sinks off Krapets
During the emergency meeting of the Security Council under the Council of Ministers, information was received about a second vessel that had been struck. It was located approximately 17 nautical miles east of Krapets and sank. According to preliminary information, one crew member was rescued. The materials provided contain no confirmed information regarding the vessel's identity, the total number of people on board or the fate of the remaining crew members.
“Another Attack Is Absolutely Unacceptable”
“Another attack against merchant ships in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters is absolutely unacceptable,” Prime Minister Rumen Radev stated.
The Prime Minister announced that Bulgaria would seek an explanation from Russian Ambassador Eleonora Mitrofanova. He clarified that, at present, there is no conclusive evidence establishing the origin of the drones that would allow responsibility for the attacks to be attributed to a specific country.
Radev stated that Bulgaria's permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union had been informed of the incidents. A conversation with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte is also forthcoming.
“The logic of what is happening indicates that the outcome of the attacks benefits the Russian Federation,” the Prime Minister stated, emphasising that this was the reason he intended to speak with the Russian ambassador.
Bulgaria Seeks International Assistance
The government will seek international support for an investigation into the strikes against three ships attacked near Bulgarian territorial waters, with the aim of establishing the origin of the drones used.
The stated priorities include strengthening surveillance of the airspace and maritime domain and enhancing national capabilities to respond to similar incidents. Bulgarian authorities have notified their partners in NATO and the European Union.
At present, the information provided confirms the evacuation of the CHELSEA 3 crew, the sinking of a second vessel off Krapets and the Prime Minister's intention to hold talks with the Russian ambassador and the NATO Secretary General. The origin of the drones and the circumstances surrounding the attacks have not been conclusively established. I BGNES
