articles.title: A divided southern flank faces Trump 2.0 and NATO 3.0 - Brookings
articles.summary: A divided southern flank faces Trump 2.0 and NATO 3.0  Brookings
articles.full_text:
The Trump administration and some Northern and Eastern European allies have criticized southern NATO members for not taking the Russian threat—and the demands of alliance solidarity—seriously. This criticism matters more as NATO becomes, in Secretary General Mark Rutte’s words, “more European”: a “NATO 3.0” in which European allies are expected to do more while the United States does less. Yet every NATO member on the southern flank has increased defense spending since 2016, and even more since 2022. Even Spain, the only member to resist NATO’s new target of spending at least 5% on defense and defense-related investments, has nearly doubled defense spending as a share of GDP since 2022, despite Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s public defiance of U.S. President Donald Trump. The focus on how much southern NATO members spend, however, risks obscuring a more important question: how effectively are they contributing to regional security?
Southern NATO members—Portugal, Spain, France, Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Montenegro, Albania, Greece and Turkey—perceive the Russian threat differently than their northern and eastern counterparts. Public opinion polls suggest that while majorities in most countries on the southern flank reject Russia’s war of aggression and therefore support aiding Ukraine, they do not see Russia as an imminent threat to their own security. This helps explain why most Southern Europeans do not seem to support massive and rapid increases in defense spending. The more critical issue is the southern NATO members’ inability or unwillingness to coordinate their strategic assets. Currently, southern NATO member states are too often focused on what divides them rather than what they might do better together.
A divided southern flank
The integration of Europe’s southern states into the Atlantic alliance was never problem-free. Italy and Portugal were both founding members of NATO in 1949, but Italian membership was opposed by those who wanted an exclusively Atlantic-facing alliance. Portugal, because of the Azores Islands, was vital for control of the Atlantic, but the authoritarian Estado Novo government was an awkward fit in an alliance of liberal democracies. NATO’s 1952 enlargement to Greece and Turkey was seen by critics as importing an unresolved conflict into the alliance and as moving it too close to the Middle East. Spain joined NATO in 1982, but its continued membership required a national referendum four years later, in which 52.5% voted in favor and 39.8% against. Indeed, resistance to NATO membership has arisen also from within the south: in Spain, Portugal, France, Italy, Greece, and Turkey, there have been political movements, chiefly on the far left or right, arguing that neutrality serves the national interest better. They may grow, fueled by a global wave of nativist populism.
While it’s apparent that Europe’s southern alliance members have to quickly catch up after years of relatively low defense spending, this is not due to their lack of commitment to NATO. Instead, it is explained by these countries’ low threat perceptions combined with pressure from key allies (like Germany) during the 2011 fiscal crisis to enact draconian spending cuts. Greece was the exception; ironically, at the time, Athens was harshly criticized for “overspending” on defense, despite its location in the conflict-prone Eastern Mediterranean. Now the South is catching up with a degree of fiscal caution that may be excessive, but its recent experience with budgetary crises makes it understandable. Domestic politics also matters: right-of-center governments tend to spend more on defense. But what matters most, given tight budgets, is threat perception: proximity to an aggressive Russia correlates well with how much of GDP European states are spending on defense.
Although Russia’s gray-zone warfare in Europe is intensifying, Southern Europe has seen significantly fewer serious incidents than Northern or Eastern Europe. Portugal, for instance, has recorded Russian cyberattacks, while Spanish authorities believe Russian operatives carried out a targeted assassination. Nonetheless, the southern flank faces growing risks: Moscow backs anti-Western military juntas across the Sahel, whose violence has previously triggered refugee flows northward, while increased Russian naval activity in the Atlantic and the Mediterranean threatens critical subsea cables. According to reporting by El Mundo, the CIA has alerted European governments of the risk of drones being launched against Spain, France, and Italy from the Russian shadow fleet operating in the Mediterranean.
Working around Southern Europe’s divisions
Of course, Southern Europe is not homogeneous. This is where the flexibility of minilateralism becomes so useful. For instance, bilateral relations with Washington vary across NATO’s southern flank. They have visibly improved with Turkey and Greece in recent years but have deteriorated markedly with Spain and, more recently and to a lesser extent, Italy. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who is ideologically close to Trump, has made clear that “being your friend has certainly not helped” her popularity.
Smaller powers such as Portugal and Greece have too much to lose from a rupture with the United States, while medium powers such as France, Spain, Italy, and Turkey appear to believe they have more room to hedge or criticize the current administration. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Greece and Portugal in October 2026 publicly displayed appreciation for allies that had allowed the United States access to military bases denied by other countries. The visits also sought to reinforce these partnerships, including through weapons procurement.
From spending to strategy
Where does this leave the southern flank as the Trump administration compels NATO 3.0 to take on the burden of Europe’s conventional defense? Many Southern Europeans hope that this is an episode in the alliance’s long history, rather than a period of permanent U.S. unreliability or hostility. But hope is not a strategy. There will be no return to the past. Europe will need to do more than increase investment in additional capabilities: It will need to develop independent strategic thinking and conceive of a European way of warfare that does not rely on or attempt to replicate U.S. weapons systems and doctrines. Finally, Europe’s collective action problem in foreign and defense policy means that coalitions of the willing are the most realistic shortcut to reordering regional security without significant U.S. involvement. Unfortunately, this is precisely where Southern Europe is weakest.
Turning capabilities into collective strength
What could be done to improve security coordination in Southern Europe? One existing minilateral format already covers most of it: the so-called Med9, inaugurated as the Med7 in 2016. It brings together all of the European Union’s (EU) southern states, from Portugal to Cyprus, and held its latest annual summit of heads of government in October 2026 in Split, Croatia. Turkey, as well as other NATO members not in the EU, are not part of this grouping, whose original purpose was to offer a counterpoint to the “Frugal Four” (Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands, and Sweden) on EU economic governance. Its scope, however, has since widened, with recent agendas and final statements increasingly alluding to security challenges.
Regular meetings of Med9 defense ministers would be the next logical step. They could provide an opening for political dialogue to bridge differences in threat perceptions across the south, particularly between the Eastern and Western Mediterranean, and to identify shared security concerns. These should include maritime security, from port and coastal defense to securing key routes; air defense, including counter-drone capabilities; threats from the Sahel and North Africa; migration management; and the protection of critical infrastructure.
If a Europeanized NATO is to be more than a slogan, southern NATO commands and brigades must be revised, turning capabilities that exist largely on paper into fighting forces that can operate with European assets and troops. Some of the most relevant challenges are discussed by Carlo Masala and Michael O’Hanlon.
Subregional groupings could help. The 5+5 Defense Initiative brings together 10 littoral nations in the Western Mediterranean—five European and five North African—to discuss soft security and confidence-building. Its four NATO members—Portugal, Spain, France, and Italy—could and should build on that experience by coordinating regular staff talks, exercises, and planning for regional deterrence and defense. Ideally, a similar arrangement would be created for the Adriatic and the Eastern Mediterranean, if Greece and Turkey could be convinced to work together.
So far, though, new developments have been limited and bilateral. Portugal and Greece, for example, have decided to buy new frigates from Italy and to hold defense consultations with Rome. Some Southern Europeans, sensitive to the negative perceptions often associated with the south, seem to fear being associated with any southern grouping. This represents a significant missed opportunity.
Southern European countries could contribute more to NATO 3.0. They could provide strategic depth for reserves, production, and logistics against threats to the east or north; play a key role in providing maritime security and securing routes for critical raw materials; and act as a barrier against threats from the south. It would require not just more investment but a degree of regional coordination that Southern Europe has not even begun to pursue. At a time of proliferating tensions and conflicts—and an explosion of minilateralism elsewhere in Europe—this inertia is baffling. The alternative is stark: Southern Europe will continue to be strategically defined by others and potentially defended by no one. Southern Europeans sho

If you think Europe's defense strategy is just talk, NATO's top brass wants you to think again. General Alexus Grynkewich just drew a hard line in Warsaw, making it clear that testing the Western military alliance is a catastrophic miscalculation.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, the NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe didn't mince words. He laid out a direct military blueprint designed to block, blunt, and break any adversary foolish enough to cross alliance borders. While he skipped explicitly naming Moscow in every single sentence, the message hit home against a backdrop of rising hybrid attacks, cyber intrusions, and escalating tensions across Eastern Europe.
The Strategy Behind the Warning
Grynkewich's pitch wasn't your standard diplomatic boilerplate. He introduced a stark military doctrine centered on absolute denial. The plan relies on a three-pronged operational framework:
- Block initial border incursions or frontline movements.
- Blunt the momentum of the assaulting force before it can gain operational breathing room.
- Break the wider military system and logistical networks supporting the offensive.
"If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight," Grynkewich stated. The goal is simple. Make sure any aggression against a member state proves completely pointless.
Why the Rhetoric Matters Now
Europe isn't just worried about all-out tank divisions rolling across borders anymore. Intelligence officials across the continent point to a steady drumbeat of low-level hybrid warfare. Sabotage attempts, mysterious arson cases, drone incursions, and crippling cyberattacks have put the alliance's one billion citizens on edge.
Grynkewich addressed these fears head-on. He admitted that recent sabotage campaigns created widespread nervousness among everyday citizens. By going public with his operational posture, he wanted to send a message to potential aggressors while offering reassurance to the public.
Behind closed doors, anxiety runs deeper than just hybrid threats. European capitals have spent months sweating over Washington's long-term commitment to mutual defense, especially with shifting political winds under U.S. President Donald Trump. Questions over whether future American administrations will back the alliance's Article 5 guarantee keep diplomats awake at night.
To combat those doubts, Grynkewich pointed directly to his own role and recent diplomatic signals, recalling supportive statements made by Trump during leadership summits. When reporters asked what keeps him awake at night, his answer was blunt. "Nothing keeps me awake at night. My job is to keep others awake."
The Realities of Deterrence
Deterrence only works if the enemy believes you can and will pull the trigger. For years, critics argued that bureaucratic delays and fractured European defense budgets left weak spots in the alliance's armor.
Russia has repeatedly denied involvement in ongoing hybrid sabotage across Europe, framing accusations as Western propaganda. Meanwhile, Moscow's threats regarding nuclear retaliation and regional flashpoints like the Kaliningrad exclave keep the pressure high.
Yet NATO's updated posture signals a shift from passive containment to active denial. Grynkewich made it clear that a defensive alliance doesn't mean a passive target. If an adversary thinks they can nibble away at alliance territory through gray-zone tactics without triggering a severe response, they are gambling with ruin.
Security analysts note that deterrence is an ongoing test of nerves. Words matter, but industrial capacity, troop readiness, and political unity matter more. The alliance is betting that spelling out a clear operational penalty will keep the peace where diplomacy alone falls short.

articles.title: ‘We still love you’: NATO envoy seeks to reassure Europe over US military pullback - Yahoo News UK
articles.summary: ‘We still love you’: NATO envoy seeks to reassure Europe over US military pullback  Yahoo News UK
articles.full_text:
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker told European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius that Washington remains committed to Europe's defence, amid an ongoing US military review withdrawing thousands of troops and key strategic assets from the continent.
"We still love you," Whitaker said at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday in the Polish capital.
"I keep telling our European allies… the United States isn't stepping back."
His remarks came during a panel on NATO 3.0 — a US-backed model that calls for Europe to take the lead with its conventional defences as American forces draw down from the continent and shift their attention elsewhere.
Kubilius said NATO 3.0 did not mean the United States was saying, "We don't love you anymore, Europeans, so you should do your own job". Rather, he argued, Europe needed to develop the capabilities to deter aggression on its own territory.
"Europe needs to take responsibility in our hands," he said.
Kubilius has previously estimated that replacing US strategic military assets could cost Europe up to €500 billion. Experts have also suggested that Europe could need 300,000 additional troops to defend itself against Russia in a scenario in which Washington continues to withdraw its military support.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, Washington has sought to redirect military resources towards other regions, including the Indo-Pacific, to counter China's growing influence.
The Pentagon's review of US military deployments in Europe is expected to conclude by December, with its findings to be presented to US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. The assessment could pave the way for further reductions in America's military presence on the continent.
However, separate force reductions are already under way. In May, for example, the Pentagon ordered the withdrawal of approximately 5,000 troops from Germany and cancelled a planned deployment of a long-range fires battalion.
Whitaker said he did not want to "preview" further measures under the review because "it is not ready", but argued that Washington's push for a more European NATO was "working".
"The proof is in where we're sitting today, here in Poland, spending 4.7% on core defence and leading really the alliance to a stronger, more capable military," he said.
Allies agreed to raise their core defence spending target from 2% to 3.5% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035 at the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, alongside a further 1.5% for broader security and defence spending.
"That is what the United States is expecting from all of its allies," Whitaker said of the overall 5% defence spending target.
Poland is among NATO's highest spenders on core defence as a share of GDP, according to the alliance's latest estimates.
The effort to increase defence spending also comes as the European Union seeks to strengthen its military capabilities by 2030, amid warnings from European intelligence agencies that Russia could pose a more direct threat to NATO in the coming years.
But the rearmament drive is facing significant hurdles. A leaked version of the European Defence Agency's landmark report — aiming to assess the progress — reveals major capability gaps, most notably in drone defences and maritime warfare.

articles.title: Expelled five years ago after the espionage scandal between Sofia and Moscow, REL: Russian diplomat expelled from Bulgaria appears in Serbia - Balkanweb.com
articles.summary: Expelled five years ago after the espionage scandal between Sofia and Moscow, REL: Russian diplomat expelled from Bulgaria appears in Serbia  Balkanweb.com
articles.full_text:
Russian diplomat Aleksandr Aleksandrovich Krasii was accredited this year as assistant military attaché to Serbia, five years after Bulgarian media reported that he had been expelled from the country as part of a spy scandal that erupted between Sofia and Moscow.
Data leaked from Russian databases shows that Aleksandr Krasii has ties to Russia's military intelligence service (GRU), Systema, the Russian-language investigative unit of Radio Free Europe (RFE/RL), has learned.
Neither the Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs nor the Bulgarian Prosecutor's Office responded to REL's request for information regarding the case.
REL's research shows that Krasii was in Serbia for about a year after his expulsion from Bulgaria, but his name appeared on the diplomatic list as assistant military attaché only in 2026.
The Russian diplomat was expelled amid an investigation in Bulgaria into a series of explosions at weapons depots, which at the time were suspected of being carried out by Russian nationals.
Moscow denied any involvement in these incidents.
Former diplomat and consultant on geopolitical and security issues, Nikolla Llunic, told REL that this case shows that the stance of Serbian institutions towards this issue, which has been present for a long time, has not changed.
"The security services must carry out the duty assigned to them by the Constitution and protect the state from a security and counterintelligence perspective. You [REL] pointed this out in 2023, but the institutions did not react in any way," Llunic said.
In a previous 2023 investigation, REL identified three Russian diplomats who began their diplomatic missions in Serbia after being expelled or blacklisted by European Union countries in the months following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
At the time, REL determined that one of them had ties to a unit of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), accused of cyberattacks on the United States energy sector, while another had ties to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service.
One of them continues to serve as a Russian diplomat in Serbia.
The media revealed the diplomat's identity
Bulgaria's Ministry of Foreign Affairs expelled another Russian diplomat at the end of April 2021.
As stated in a statement issued on April 29, the expulsion was part of a series of expulsions, while the Russian ambassador was summoned for talks.
Although the ministry did not disclose his identity, Bulgarian media revealed it.
The private news agency Zona News and the Bulgarian public broadcaster reported two days later that it was Lieutenant Colonel Aleksandr Krasii, who was an assistant to the Russian military attaché.
Zona News said it had received this information "from its sources," while later stating that the public broadcaster had received the information from it without citing the source.
The agency reported that Krasii was supposed to leave Bulgaria no later than May 5th.
According to Bulgarian National Television, Krasii became a diplomat of that country at the end of 2020 and arrived in Bulgaria at the beginning of 2021.
It was also reported that during his four-month stay, he had only made one public engagement: on behalf of Russian Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu, he had presented a decoration to an activist of the Russophile association in Bulgaria.
The association's website published a report on the event, as well as a photo of Krasii with its members.
REL did not receive a response from Bulgarian National Television or Zona News regarding how they determined that Krasii was the expelled diplomat, while the Russophile association did not respond regarding his expulsion from Bulgaria either.
From Bulgaria to Serbia
A little over a year after the expulsion, Krasii was photographed at an event at the University of Defense in Belgrade.
He was photographed among instructors and participants attending advanced training at the National Defense School, a military educational institution.
REL identified Krasii, among other things, based on the markings on the uniform he wore at that event, which read "AA Krasii".
The name Aleksandar Krasii first appeared on the diplomatic list in 2026. This list is the official register of foreign diplomats, which is periodically updated and published by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Serbia.
That same year, REL identified him at two events in Belgrade.
In April, he attended a wreath-laying ceremony before a meeting of the Serbian-Russian Intergovernmental Committee for Trade, Economic and Scientific-Technical Cooperation.
A few weeks later, in May, he was photographed taking part in the "Immortal Regiment" march, a ceremony that originated in Russia, where it was first organized in 2012 to commemorate Red Army soldiers killed during World War II.
The Serbian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Russian Embassy did not respond to REL's request for comment regarding Krasii's diplomatic mission in Serbia.
Deported amid investigation into explosions and poisoning
Krasii was deported from Bulgaria amid an investigation in which six Russian citizens were accused of involvement in a series of explosions that occurred over a ten-year period.
At the time, Bulgarian prosecutors stated that there was a “reasonable suspicion” that explosions that hit four warehouses and production facilities in Bulgaria between 2011 and 2020 were linked to the poisoning of Bulgarian arms dealer Emilian Gebrev in 2015, as well as an explosion at ammunition depots in the Czech Republic in 2014.
A spokesman for the Prosecutor General's Office stated at the time that it could be concluded that "the purpose of the actions of Russian citizens was to interrupt the supply of special products to Georgia and Ukraine."
In 2015, arms dealer Emilian Gebrev began vomiting during dinner at a restaurant in Sofia. He was then taken to a military hospital, where he experienced severe hallucinations and fell into a coma. His son also fell ill suddenly, as did the director of Gebrev's arms trading company EMCO.
Gebrev eventually recovered.
At the time, investigators linked the entire case to the Czech Republic. In 2021, the country accused Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, of being behind an October 2014 act of sabotage in the town of Vrbetice, where 50 tons of ammunition exploded and two people died.
The Bulgarian Prosecutor's Office did not respond to REL regarding the progress of the aforementioned investigation or whether Russian diplomat Aleksandr Krasii is also part of it.
Addresses of Russian intelligence officers
Krasii's connections to Russia's military intelligence service are indicated by his addresses, Systema has learned.
In most leaked Russian databases, including, for example, the state services database “Gosuslugi”, the data of one of the largest private laboratories in Russia, Gemotest, as well as a health insurance database, Krasii lists his residential address as “Devichye Pole, no. 4”, in Moscow.
This is not a residential building, but the headquarters of the Joint Academy of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, one of Russia's leading military educational institutions.
It appears that Krasii has only given his real address on a few occasions.
One such case was when he applied for so-called “COVID permits,” introduced in 2020 and required for movement around Moscow during the lockdown. For these permits, applicants had to provide the departure and arrival points of their trips.
In all five permits Krasii received in the spring of 2020, the starting point was an address on “Marshal Biryuzov” Street: once without a building number, once with the number 2, once with the number 7, and twice with the number 4.
According to investigative journalists, the latter address houses apartments for the families of officers studying at the so-called "Conservatory", or the Military Diplomatic Academy.
Many future officers and operatives of the Russian military intelligence, the GRU, graduated from this academy and lived at that address. Among them is Anatoly Chepiga, who took part in the attempted poisoning of Russian double agent Sergei Skripal in 2018 in Salisbury, England.
Considering that, according to Bulgarian media reports, Krasii was already assigned to the Russian consulate in Bulgaria at the end of 2020, it seems that his assignment there occurred immediately after completing his studies at the “Conservatory”.
According to leaked data, Krasii spent almost two years, from 2013 to 2015, in the town of Gorny, in the Russian Zabaikalsky Krai.
Gorny is one of about 40 closed cities in Russia, meaning that special permission is required to enter it.
Gorny is closed because until 2002 it was home to the 4th Strategic Missile Division of Russia's Strategic Missile Forces.
The division was later disbanded, and according to official data, Gorny is currently home to several units of the Russian Armed Forces, none of which are related to strategic missiles or nuclear weapons. However, Gorny has retained its status as a closed city to this day.
This is not the first known case where GRU officers serving abroad have previously lived in closed military towns in Russia.
GRU officer Yuri Mikheev, who operates under diplomatic cover in African countries, lived from 2010 to 2015 in the closed town of Ozerny, in the Tver region, which, like Gorny, is linked to Russia's Strategic Missile Forces.
Another expelled diplomat remains in Serbia
Krasii is not the only Russian diplomat who, after being expelled from an EU country, ended up in a diplomatic mission in Serbia.
Hundreds of Russian diplomats were expelled from EU member states or blacklisted in the months following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
REL found that at least three of these diplomats became accredited representatives of Russia in Serbia, including two who had ties to Russian intelligence services.
Russian diplomats were not expelled from Serbia in 2022 because, unlike most European countries, Serbia did not impose sanctions on Moscow

articles.title: America Shouldn’t Let Go of the Middle East
articles.summary: Why disengagement is not the answer.
articles.full_text:
Michael Corleone’s famous lament in The Godfather, Part III could serve as a motto for every American president of the past three decades when it comes to the Middle East: “Just when I thought I was out, they pull me back in.” Bill Clinton promised to focus “like a laser beam” on the economy but would spend the end of his presidency consumed by the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and trying to contain Saddam Hussein’s Iraq. George W. Bush came to office pledging a “humble” foreign policy and ended up invading and occupying Afghanistan and Iraq. Barack Obama announced a “pivot to Asia,” only to be drawn into the aftermath of the Arab Spring, a military campaign against the Islamic State (or ISIS), and an all-consuming negotiation with Iran. Joe Biden tried to deprioritize the region—until Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel consumed much of Biden’s presidency. And most strikingly, Donald Trump, having campaigned against “endless wars,” has ended up gambling on a reckless war against Iran that could define his second term.
The Iran war has given new impetus to a long-standing debate about U.S. policy in the Middle East. Writing in Foreign Affairs in August, Michael Fuchs argued that the conflict—an “epic disaster”—should spur a long-overdue withdrawal. The United States, he contends, should pull all its bases and forces out of the region and “end its role as guarantor of regional order,” freeing Washington to concentrate on higher-priority objectives in Asia and Europe. It is a serious argument that will resonate with the many Americans who have watched their country spend trillions of dollars and sacrifice thousands of lives in the region with little to show for it.
This diagnosis of U.S. overcommitment is right. But the prescription of “letting go”—and essentially leaving the region to its fate—is not. The Iran war has not demonstrated that the United States no longer has interests in the Middle East; it has demonstrated, very painfully, that it does and that the way Washington has been pursuing them for a generation is unsustainable. The lesson is not to abandon the region but to rethink an approach that has become both too costly and counterproductive. The United States should instead defend a narrower set of core interests with a smaller military footprint, more diplomacy, more alternatives, and more partners. Neither doubling down nor walking away offers a way out of the cycle that has trapped every recent president. A more pragmatic and disciplined middle course might.
FOREIGN FOLLIES
Consider what critics of U.S. foreign policy in the region get right. The wars in Afghanistan and Iraq cost at least $2 trillion each, along with the lives of thousands of U.S. service members and hundreds of thousands of local civilians. The wars severely tarnished the United States’ global reputation and left a generation of Americans skeptical that the country could be a force for good in the world. Twenty-five years of counterterrorism operations did significantly degrade the global terrorist threat, but they also left the region no freer and, in many places, less stable. Now the Iran war has added new consequences of U.S. hubris and military overreach: tens of billions of dollars in direct military costs, thousands killed or wounded, the diversion of military assets from other vital regions, depleted stocks of scarce munitions, strained alliances, a windfall for Russia from higher oil prices, an even more hard-line Iranian regime, and the biggest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market.
The critics are also right that the U.S. military presence in the region, which was long considered essential for deterring war and keeping energy flowing, has in many ways become a liability. The network of large bases that Washington built after the 1991 Gulf War is now vulnerable to Iranian drones and ballistic missiles, offering Tehran targets and leverage rather than deterring it from taking military action. Forward-deployed forces, meanwhile, tempt U.S. leaders to reach for military solutions, and the need to protect those forces creates a self-defeating loop in which the threat to U.S. forces becomes a large part of the rationale for keeping them there. And critics are right that U.S. support for regional partners has been too easy to take for granted and too easily abused. Washington’s almost unconditional backing for Israel, for example, has created a moral hazard—an implicit insurance policy that encourages Israeli risk-taking and draws the United States into conflicts it did not choose and cannot control. The U.S. dependence on Gulf partners to maintain its security presence has likewise led to Washington’s muted criticism of repression and acquiescence to destabilizing interventions in places such as Libya, Sudan, and Yemen.
As a result, U.S. domestic politics are moving in the direction of restraint if not outright withdrawal. A large majority of Americans tell pollsters that the Iran war is not worth fighting, and voters in both parties, especially younger ones, are increasingly skeptical of the U.S. security partnership with Israel and of “forever wars” that do not seem to make the country safer or address the issues they care most about. Any strategy that ignores that skepticism is unlikely to survive the next election or to be funded by the Congress that is likely to emerge from it.
THE INTERESTS ABIDE
Acknowledging that U.S. policy has failed, however, is not the same as concluding that U.S. interests have vanished. Some of the most important reasons for past American engagement in the region—for example, Cold War competition with the Soviet Union, heavy U.S. dependence on imported oil, threats from al-Qaeda and ISIS at their peak, and a vulnerable Israel’s need for protection against hostile Arab armies—have indeed faded. But the interests that remain are real, as the Iran war has so vividly illustrated.
Take the continued importance of energy supplies. The United States is now a net exporter of oil and gas and imports little crude from the Persian Gulf, leading many to conclude that the region’s energy no longer matters much to Americans. But the notion of U.S. “energy independence” is vastly overstated. Oil is a fungible commodity with a single global price. As the Iran war has shown, when supplies are cut anywhere, Americans pay more at the pump, and slower growth in Asia and Europe drags down the U.S. economy, too. Nor is the world weaning itself off fossil fuels as quickly as many had hoped. Despite the real boom in renewables such as solar, wind, and hydropower, global consumption of oil and coal recently reached an all-time high, and fossil fuels still supply roughly 80 percent of the world’s energy, down only modestly from around 85 percent in the early 1990s. The relentless spread of energy-hungry data centers is pushing demand higher still.
The Iran war has been a brutal reminder of these realities. Iran predictably responded to U.S. and Israeli strikes by attacking regional energy infrastructure and closing off shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, through which a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil trade and nearly a fifth of its liquefied natural gas had flowed, along with fertilizer, refined products, and other critical goods. Oil prices spiked, leading U.S. gasoline prices to rise by more than 40 percent, and diesel by more than 70 percent, fueling inflation and pushing up interest rates. Only a combination of surprisingly sharp Chinese oil import cuts (facilitated by stockpiling and a pivot toward renewables), emergency releases from strategic petroleum reserves, and Saudi and Emirati pipelines that bypass the Strait has kept the damage from being far worse—for now. When contemplating whether the United States still needs to care about oil flowing out of the Middle East, it is worth remembering that a one percent annual decline in U.S. GDP triggered by an oil-supply shock would cost the United States over $300 billion in lost output; a one percent hit to global output would cost the world over $1 trillion. Those are consequences all Americans should care about.
 The United States has positive interests in the region, not just threats to avert.
Nuclear nonproliferation is another enduring interest. Some scholars argue that a nuclear-armed Iran could be deterred, and even that the spread of nuclear weapons might stabilize the region, as it arguably did during the Cold War. Others believe that with the threat of U.S. military intervention removed or reduced, Iran would simply forgo the nuclear option, so there is little to worry about. Either outcome is possible, but no American president is likely to bet on it, and for good reason. A nuclear Iran would know it could maintain or increase its support for proxy forces and its meddling in its neighbors’ affairs, or escalate its conflict with Israel, confident that its arsenal would deter any attempt to overthrow the regime in response.
And if Iran got the bomb its regional neighbors would likely try to do so, as well. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who signed a mutual defense pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan in 2025 and with Turkey and Pakistan in 2026, has said that if Iran gets a nuclear weapon, Saudi Arabia will also “have to get one.” Turkey’s foreign minister said earlier this year that his country would consider doing the same. A Middle East with multiple nuclear powers, many of them rivals, would be far more dangerous than it is today, with a higher risk of a nuclear accident or nuclear weapons use. The logic of U.S. disengagement from the region implies that Washington could live with an Iranian bomb, as it lives with Pakistan’s and North Korea’s, and perhaps it could. But most Americans would probably prefer never to find out.
